sentence: I can still smell her kitchen on Sunday mornings, the cinnamon and yeast braided into the air like a benediction. She kept the butter dish under a glass dome on the windowsill, and the linoleum had a worn spot in front of the stove where she stood for sixty years. Nothing I bake now ever tastes quite right. I think it's because my hands aren't her hands, and the light through her curtains was a softer kind of gold than anything we have anymore.

The flour tin had a hand-painted rooster on the lid and lived on a shelf above the icebox. Whenever she made biscuits she would let me press the floured rim of a jelly glass into the dough and lift out the soft pale circles one by one. I remember the dusting of flour on her forearms, the talcum smell of her apron, the way she hummed without realizing she was humming.

There was a yellow Formica table in the corner where I ate countless bowls of oatmeal stirred thick with brown sugar and a single pat of melting butter. The chair legs squeaked against the linoleum and the salt shaker was always a tiny ceramic hen. She would sit across from me with her coffee, the steam curling up between us, and the morning would unfold so slowly it felt as though time had simply forgotten our house.

Her dish towels were embroidered with the days of the week, and each one was the right one only on its own day. I learned to dry the plates carefully, lifting each from the rack and turning it in my small hands while she washed and rinsed and hummed. The water from the tap ran hot in a way I have never managed to recreate in any kitchen since.

She kept butterscotch candies in a cut-glass dish on top of the refrigerator, and I had to climb on a chair to reach them, and she pretended not to know. The wrappers crinkled in my pocket all afternoon. I can still taste that particular sweetness, butter and sugar cooked just past the point of caution, and it tastes of being small and beloved and certain that the world was a fundamentally good and ordered place.

The kettle on her stove whistled with a thin, complaining note that I associated, then and now, with the particular safety of an afternoon indoors. She poured tea into thin porcelain cups so old the gilt had worn away from the rims. I would sit at the window watching the snow come down over the hedges, and the radiator hissed, and her knitting needles clicked, and nothing in the world needed to happen.

She had a recipe box made of tin with hinges that squeaked, full of index cards yellowed at the corners and stained with vanilla and butter. Her handwriting tilted forward as though leaning into the next word. I keep that box on my own counter now and I sometimes open it just to see her name signed at the bottom of a pie crust recipe she copied from her own mother in 1952.

The cabinets were painted a soft mint green that had grown softer and greener with each repainting. When you opened them they smelled faintly of nutmeg and old wood and the brown paper she lined the shelves with every spring. I have spent years trying to find a green like that, and the truth is the green isn't the thing. The thing is her hand on the cabinet door, and her wedding ring catching the light.

She made jam every August in a great copper pot, and the whole kitchen filled with the dense red steam of strawberries surrendering their summer. The jars cooled on the windowsill with their little tin lids, and I remember the soft pop each one made as the seal pulled tight overnight. I would lie in the spare bedroom listening for those soft punctuations, and they felt like the house itself making promises.

The radio on the windowsill was always tuned to the same station, and at noon a man with a voice like worn leather would read the obituaries and the weather. She would stop whatever she was doing and listen. I didn't understand the gravity of it then, the way she nodded at certain names. I understand now. I think of her every time I hear an old man's voice on a small kitchen radio, and I miss her with a particular and useless tenderness.

Summer evenings stretched themselves out as if reluctant to end. We rode our bikes in slow loops at the end of the cul-de-sac while our mothers called us in one by one, voices floating across yards that smelled of cut grass and barbecue smoke. The streetlights would tick on with their small pink hesitation, and we knew we had maybe ten more minutes. Those ten minutes were the longest, sweetest minutes of the year.

I remember the particular blue of the sky just after the sun went down, when the air cooled all at once and you could smell sprinklers running on three streets at once. We played freeze tag in someone's front yard until we couldn't see each other anymore, and even then we kept playing, navigating by laughter and the white of someone's t-shirt. I think about those evenings more often than I should.

The lightning bugs came out at dusk and we caught them in mason jars with holes punched in the lids by my father with a screwdriver. They blinked slowly on our nightstands while we fell asleep, and in the morning they were always gone, though the jars sat empty on the windowsill all day. I never asked where they went. I think I knew, in some small way, that summer wasn't going to last forever either.

After dinner the neighborhood emptied into the warm dark like a held breath being slowly let out. Someone's father would be grilling, someone's older sister would be smoking on the porch, the cicadas would be working themselves up into their evening hymn. We were too young to belong to anything but the moment, and we belonged to it absolutely, and we have never quite belonged to anything that completely since.

The sound of an ice cream truck two streets over could empty our house in seconds. I would stand barefoot on the warm pavement with two quarters in my fist, watching the truck approach with its tinny circus music. The popsicles came in paper sleeves and stained your tongue blue or red for an hour. I have eaten finer desserts in finer cities, but none of them tasted of anything that mattered.

We lay on our backs in the grass and watched the first stars come out one at a time, and you could feel the earth holding the day's heat against your shoulder blades. My friend's mother would bring out lemonade in a sweating pitcher, and we would drink it too fast and get the brain-aches that we found unaccountably funny. The whole world was the size of one yard and large enough.

The sprinklers ran in tick-tock arcs over the lawns and we ran through them in shorts and t-shirts until our skin was cool and our hair smelled like chlorine and grass clippings. The water from the hose tasted faintly of rubber and metal, and it was the best water that has ever existed. I have walked through too many beautiful gardens since, and none of them have been a sprinkler.

Sometimes the older kids would build a fire in someone's backyard pit and we would sit at the edge of the circle, allowed in but not yet of them, watching sparks travel up into the sky and disappear. Their conversations were thrilling and incomprehensible. I remember thinking that being fifteen would feel exactly like that fire looked, and being grateful for the wait.

My mother used to leave the kitchen window open all evening, and I could hear the radio playing softly while I was outside, and I knew she was in there washing dishes and listening to a baseball game and waiting for me to come in. That sound, the radio and the running water and the cicadas all braided together, is what summer means to me, and I don't think anything will ever replace it.

We made plans for the next day that we mostly forgot by morning, but the planning itself was the point: standing in a circle of bicycles under a streetlight, arguing about whose backyard was best for the fort, debating whether we needed a treasure map. We were the kings and queens of small things, and the small things were everything, and the dark closed around us with such gentle attention that I can almost feel it on my arms even now.

Our first apartment had crooked floors and a window that wouldn't quite shut, and we loved it with an embarrassing completeness. The kitchen counter held exactly two coffee mugs and a colander. We owned three forks. On Sundays we made pancakes from a box and watched the light move across the bare wall like a slow visitor, and we couldn't have been happier if someone had handed us a kingdom.

The radiator clanked like someone was hammering it with a wrench, but the heat was free and we let it run all winter. I remember the particular smell of that hallway, varnish and old plaster and somebody's curry, and how the key stuck in the lock and you had to lift the door slightly before you turned it. We learned that move so well our hands still remember it.

We had a record player on a milk crate and a mattress on the floor and a poster of a museum exhibit neither of us had attended. I remember standing in the middle of the empty living room the day we got the keys and laughing because it was so small and so ours. We didn't know yet how much we would miss those four hundred square feet, or how the rest of our lives would have to live up to that single bright winter.

The bathroom had black-and-white hexagon tiles and a clawfoot tub that took twenty minutes to fill. I used to read in there with the door open so I could hear the kettle whistle in the kitchen. We drank an absurd amount of tea that year. I think we were trying to feel like adults, and the tea was part of the costume, and the costume eventually became the person.

Our neighbor on the third floor played saxophone every evening at six, and at first it was annoying and then it was a clock, and then it was a friend. We never met him. I remember thinking we would, eventually, and then the lease ended and we moved across the country and we never did. He is still playing in my memory at six o'clock every evening, and I am still listening through the floorboards.

We bought a single houseplant from the corner bodega and named it after a poet and watered it conscientiously and it died in three weeks. We were heartbroken in a way that now seems disproportionate but felt enormous at the time. We were trying so hard, then, to keep things alive. We were trying so hard to be the people we were becoming.

On Friday nights we would buy a four-dollar bottle of wine and walk it back through the cold and uncork it on the fire escape and feel like we had figured out the secret to civilization. The city was loud below us and we were quiet above it and the bottle never lasted past midnight. I would give a great deal to be that broke and that certain again, just for one evening.

I remember the woman at the bodega downstairs who learned our names within a week. She kept a tabby cat on the counter and gave us a free banana whenever we bought eggs. The store is a nail salon now. I walked past it last spring and stood across the street and tried to remember exactly where the cat had sat, and I couldn't be sure, and I felt like I had failed at something important.

The light in that living room came in slantwise through one east-facing window for about forty minutes each morning, and during that brief window the dust in the air looked like something a director had asked for. I used to drink my coffee in that light and watch the steam catch in it. I don't think I knew, then, that I was being given anything. I think I just knew that the morning was beautiful.

We hosted a dinner party with seven people in our four-hundred-square-foot kitchen and we had to wash the wine glasses between courses because we only owned four. People sat on the windowsill and the floor and one person sat in the bathtub. I have hosted larger and finer dinners since, on tables that fit everyone, and none of them have felt as much like a celebration of anything as that one did.

When we finally moved out I stood in the empty living room one last time and the late sun came in the way it always had, and I understood for the first time that places leave you the way people do. I locked the door and slid the keys under it and walked down the stairs and out into the rest of my life, and the building behind me became, in that instant, a memory.

Main Street ran four blocks and held everything we needed. The hardware store had a wooden floor that creaked, the bakery sold bread still warm at noon, and the barber knew your father's name and your father's father's. The streetlamps were the old iron kind with green glass globes, and at dusk they came on with a faint hum. I cannot pass a green glass globe in any city without my chest tightening.

The diner on the corner had a counter with red vinyl stools that spun if you pushed off hard enough, and the coffee came in heavy white mugs that warmed your hands. The waitress called everyone honey, and she meant it. The jukebox played the same fifteen songs and we never tired of any of them. I drove through that town last spring and the diner was gone, and there was a coffee shop where it had stood, and I did not go in.

The five-and-dime had everything: pencils and goldfish and ribbon and embroidery hoops and a popcorn machine that smelled like the entire week of every week. The wooden floor had a slight rise near the back where you could feel the old foundation pushing up. I bought my first paperback there for thirty-five cents. I still have it. The pages have gone the color of weak tea.

On Saturday mornings the farmers parked their trucks at an angle along the curb and sold tomatoes and corn from the beds. The smell of fresh dirt and overripe fruit hung in the air all morning. Old men in feed caps sat on the bench in front of the bank and watched the cars and waved at every one of them, whether they knew the driver or not. There was no efficiency to any of it, and that was the point.

The pharmacy still had a soda fountain in the back, and the pharmacist's daughter worked the counter on weekends. She made cherry phosphates with real syrup and a long silver spoon. I had a crush on her that I never disclosed and that she never noticed and that lasted, in some quiet form, much of one summer. I drove past the building last year and the windows were papered over, and I wished her well, wherever she was.

The movie theater had one screen and showed each film for two weeks, and on summer nights people would walk down Main Street and stop and read the marquee and decide. The lobby smelled of popcorn and carpet and air conditioning that worked too hard. The usher wore a red vest and tore your ticket in half with a ceremonial little tug. I have not torn a ticket in twenty years and I miss the small ceremony of it.

The Christmas lights went up the day after Thanksgiving and were strung between the lampposts in long swags. They came on at four-thirty when the sky was already going lavender, and the whole street took on the look of a postcard nobody had bothered to send. I used to walk my dog the long way home just to pass under them. The dog has been gone a long time now. The lights, I imagine, still go up.

The post office had brass mailboxes with little glass windows and combination locks shaped like dials from an old radio. My mother had number 247 for forty years, and I can still spin the dial in my head: seven left, twenty-two right, four left. I never have any reason to know that combination anymore, and yet my fingers remember it as if the muscle of the thing has outlasted the use of it.

The clock on top of the bank was always five minutes fast, and it had been five minutes fast for as long as anyone could remember, and we all knew to adjust. There was something companionable about the wrongness of it, the way the whole town accommodated the same gentle inaccuracy together. They fixed it the year I moved away, and I heard about it from my mother in a letter, and I felt a small mourning I could not have explained.

I went back last fall and walked the four blocks slowly, looking for ghosts. The hardware store is a wine bar now, and the bakery is a real estate office, and the barber is dead. But the light coming down Main Street at five o'clock in October was the same light, and the maples were the same maples, and for a moment I was eleven and walking home with a comic book under my arm.

The albums lived in a cabinet in the den, and we would pull them out on rainy Sunday afternoons and sit on the carpet turning the heavy black pages. The photos were held in by little black corners that you could pry off and put back, and beneath each one my grandmother had written the names and the year in white pencil. Faces I never met smiled up at me from beaches I have never seen.

There is one picture of my father at twelve standing on a dock holding a fish almost as long as his leg, grinning with the entire force of being twelve, and I love that boy with an ache I cannot put down. He doesn't know yet that he will be my father. He doesn't know about any of it. He just knows about the fish, and the sun is on his face, and the lake is behind him, and I want to walk into the picture and stand beside him.

The colors in the seventies photos have gone soft and orange, as though they were taken inside a marigold. Everyone is wearing collared shirts in colors no one wears anymore. My mother has a haircut I do not associate with her, and she is sitting on a porch with a glass of something in her hand, and she is laughing at someone outside the frame. I have wondered for years who was making her laugh.

My grandfather took most of the pictures, which is why there are so few of him. The ones we do have show him in profile, leaning into the lens of his old Leica, his face half hidden by the camera. He was always behind the thing instead of in front of it, and I think now that this was a kind of love I didn't recognize at the time, the willingness to be unseen for the sake of seeing.

There is a photograph of my parents on their honeymoon in front of a small lake hotel, both of them so young they look borrowed. My father is wearing a sport coat with patches on the elbows. My mother's hair is pinned up. They are holding hands and looking at each other with the cautious astonishment of people who have just promised something they don't entirely understand. I keep that one on my desk.

We found a shoebox of pictures in the attic after my grandmother died, and at the bottom was an envelope of photographs I had never seen: my grandmother at twenty-three, in a uniform, standing in front of a brick building with three women I did not recognize. She never told me she had been a nurse. She never told me about any of those years. The photographs are all I have, and they do not say enough.

There is a photograph of me at four in a paper hat at someone's birthday party, holding a slice of cake on a paper plate, looking very serious about the cake. I do not remember the party. I do not know whose birthday it was. But the boy in the picture is unmistakably me, and the cake is unmistakably important, and I find this whole arrangement unbearably tender every time I come across it.

The Polaroids have aged worst, going pale around the edges and almost ghostly in the center, the colors retreating like a tide. There is one of my brother and me on Christmas morning in matching pajamas in front of a tree that filled the whole corner of the living room. We are holding up identical toy trucks. We are both grinning. I think I would trade most of what I own to be inside that small bright square again, just for an hour.

My mother organized the family albums in the last summer she was well enough to do so, and her labels are precise and tender: Easter, the year of the green dress; David, his second-grade school picture, before the front tooth. I read her handwriting the way one reads a letter from someone who is no longer reachable. She was leaving me a map. She didn't tell me, and I didn't know, and now I follow it.

I scanned the albums last year so my children would have them, and the scanner whirred and the light moved across each face and I felt I was performing some small act of resurrection. But of course it is not the same. The pictures we hold in our hands have been held by other hands, and there is a kind of warmth in that I cannot transfer to a hard drive, and I know it, and I scan them anyway.

There was a time when calling another state meant something. The phone in the hallway had a long curly cord that stretched into the kitchen, and on Sunday nights my mother would dial my grandmother and twist the cord around her finger and talk for exactly fifteen minutes before the rates went up. We were lined up against the wall waiting our turns. Each of us had perhaps three minutes of grandmother before we had to hand the receiver to the next.

I remember the heft of the old rotary phone, the way you had to pull each number all the way around and wait for it to click back before dialing the next, the satisfying mechanical patience of it. Calls felt earned. You sat down to make them. You had things to say. I miss that ritual more than I would have predicted, the small theater of intention before a voice on the other end said hello.

My father called from a payphone in a Holiday Inn parking lot every Thursday when he traveled for work, and you could hear the wind and the traffic behind him. The line crackled. He sounded tinny and far away. I would tell him about my spelling test, and he would tell me he loved me, and then his quarter would run out and the line would die mid-sentence, and I would stand holding the receiver listening to the dial tone for a moment longer than I needed to.

When I went away to college my mother wrote down the time difference on a Post-it note and stuck it to the wall above the kitchen phone. She would call me on Sunday mornings, after church, and I could hear the coffee pot percolating in the background, and the dog's nails on the linoleum, and the radio playing the same station it had always played, and I could hold all of home in my ear for the length of one conversation.

There were no text messages then. If you wanted to know whether your friend got home safe, you called and let the phone ring twice and hung up, and they did the same back to you. We had whole languages built out of unanswered rings. I cannot explain to my children why a phone ringing in the next room used to feel like such a thrilling small event, like maybe the entire shape of the evening was about to change.

The phone book sat on top of the refrigerator and weighed several pounds, and finding a number meant flipping pages with a wet finger and squinting at columns of tiny print. We knew our friends' numbers by heart, all seven digits, the rhythm of them stored in the body. I cannot recall a single phone number now except the one I had in 1987. The brain holds on to such strange things.

On New Year's Eve we would call my aunt in Wisconsin at exactly midnight Eastern time, even though it was eleven for her, and she would pretend to be surprised every year. The line would be busy for the first three tries. When we finally got through, my mother would say Happy New Year, Marge, and Marge would laugh, and I remember that laugh through static like a fire heard through a wall.

I called a girl I liked from a payphone at the bus station once when I was sixteen, with a fistful of quarters and a piece of paper with her number written on it three times in case I lost it. The phone smelled like cigarettes and the booth was warm from the afternoon sun. She answered. We talked for forty minutes. I have made a great many phone calls in my life. I remember that one entirely.

The answering machine was a strange and miraculous thing, the little red light blinking in the dim kitchen when you came home. My grandfather refused to speak to one for years. He would call, hear the message, and hang up. Then he learned, and his voice came onto the tape solemn and careful, as though he were addressing a small parliament. I have one of those tapes still, in a drawer, though I no longer own anything that can play it.

The last long-distance call I made on a landline was to my mother on a Tuesday in 2007, from an apartment kitchen I no longer remember the layout of. I cannot recall what we talked about. I wish I had known it was the last one. I wish I had paid the kind of attention you save for endings. We were just having a regular conversation, the kind we had a thousand times, and then we never had another like it.

My father kept his records in milk crates beside the stereo cabinet, alphabetized by artist, the spines slightly bowed from years of pulling them out and sliding them back in. He would take a record from its sleeve with the kind of care normally reserved for relics, hold it by the edges, lower it onto the platter, and rest the needle in the groove with a small intake of breath. Then he would lean back in his chair and close his eyes, and the music would arrive.

The first thirty seconds of any record were the hiss before the first note, the soft static that meant something was about to begin. I have not heard that sound in years without feeling that I am about to be given something. The whole apparatus had a ceremony to it. You couldn't walk away in the middle of a song. You had to be there. You had to flip the record. You had to participate.

The covers were objects in themselves. I would lie on the carpet and read the liner notes and stare at the photograph on the back while the music played, learning the names of session musicians and the dates of recordings, building a small private mythology out of the personnel of a record I would never see made. The album was a place you went, not a thing you put on. I miss going there.

My uncle had a Linn turntable on a granite slab in his living room, isolated from any vibration that might disturb the needle, and he treated it the way one treats a sacrament. He would put on a record and then sit very still while it played, his hands folded in his lap. I learned, watching him, that listening could be a posture, and that attention could be a discipline, and that some things deserve both.

There was a record store downtown with a wooden floor and a black cat who slept on the jazz section, and you could spend an entire Saturday afternoon there without buying anything and the owner would not mind. He would put a record on the house turntable and let it play through, and customers would drift toward the counter and lean on it and listen and not talk, and it was the closest thing to a church I knew at seventeen.

I remember the smell of cardboard sleeves and old vinyl and the faint waxy scent of the inner paper, and how a record bought used carried the ghost of the room it had lived in: cigarettes, woodsmoke, somebody's perfume. You inherited a stranger's evenings when you bought a stranger's record. The music had been someone else's first. I always tried to imagine that someone, and sometimes I think I could almost feel them in the room with me as I listened.

When my father died I inherited his records, the crates and crates of them, and for months I could not bear to open the boxes. When I finally did, I put on the first record his hand had touched ten thousand times, and the hiss came up out of the speakers like a familiar greeting, and I sat down on the floor and listened to the whole side, and I felt him beside me in a way I have not felt him since.

There was a particular skip in our copy of a Van Morrison album, a half-second jump near the end of the second song, and we lived with it for so long that when I finally heard the song properly on someone else's stereo I felt cheated. Our version had been the right version. The skip had become part of the song. I have learned, since, that the things we love are sometimes loved precisely for their flaws.

On Saturday mornings my mother would put on a record and open all the windows, and the music would drift out across the lawn while she dusted, and I would lie in my room and listen to her sing along quietly from two rooms away. She had a clear, untrained voice. I never told her how often I lay there listening. I assumed there would be a moment to tell her, and I let the moment pass, and now I think of it whenever I open a window.

I bought my first turntable at a thrift store for twenty-two dollars, and I carried it home cradled in my arms like an infant, and I plugged it into my college roommate's stereo, and the first record I played was one I had taken from my parents' crate without permission. The needle dropped. The first note came on. I understood, for the first time, what it was my father had been doing all those years in his chair with his eyes closed.

We left at four in the morning to beat the traffic, and my brother and I sat in the back of the station wagon in our pajamas with pillows and the dog between us. The sky was still that deep predawn blue when we pulled onto the highway. My father drank coffee from a thermos. My mother passed back animal crackers. I remember the headlights coming the other way down the empty road, and the certainty that we were going somewhere wonderful.

The atlas lived in the glove compartment, and my mother would unfold it across her lap and trace our route with her finger, calling out the names of towns we would pass through. The names sounded foreign and full of promise: Wytheville, Marion, Bristol. We never stopped in any of them. They lived only as syllables and as a finger on a map, and they were the better for it.

We played the license plate game and the alphabet game and a game my brother invented where you had to spot a yellow vehicle every five miles or you lost a point, the rules of which I no longer remember but the laughter of which I can still hear. The car smelled of coffee and dog and the upholstery and whatever sandwich my mother had packed in waxed paper for lunch, and that was the smell of vacation, and no perfume since has ever come close.

The rest stops had vending machines that took only quarters and gave back warm Sprite and stale peanut butter crackers, and we treated each of these like a great delicacy. The bathrooms had hand dryers that didn't work, and the picnic tables were carved with the initials of strangers, and the dog ran wide circles on the brown grass. I remember those rest stops more clearly than the destinations.

At a certain hour the light would soften and my mother would say it was the magic hour and roll down her window and let her hand ride the wind, and my father would put on a tape, and we would all stop talking for a while, and we would just be a family in a car at sunset on a stretch of road we had never seen before, and I think now that I have been chasing that particular feeling for the rest of my life.

We stayed at motels with pools the color of swimming-pool postcards and rooms that smelled of chlorine and old carpet, and we thought they were the height of luxury. The keys were attached to plastic diamonds with the room number stamped in gold. The ice machine made a great industrial racket at the end of the hallway. I have stayed in much finer hotels since, and have never felt as thrilled by a room as I did by those.

Somewhere in Tennessee we drove through a thunderstorm so heavy the wipers couldn't keep up, and my father pulled under a highway overpass with three other cars and we all sat there in our own little caves while the rain hammered the concrete above. I remember the sudden quiet under the overpass, the smell of wet road, the rhythm of the rain on the roof. We sat there for forty minutes and nobody complained. It was, somehow, perfect.

There was a particular billboard for a diner that started two hundred miles out and counted down: Pancakes in 200 miles, Pancakes in 150 miles, Pancakes in 100. We would cheer for each one. When we finally arrived the pancakes were ordinary pancakes, but they tasted like the entire road, like the slow accumulation of anticipation, and I have not eaten pancakes that good since.

My brother and I fell asleep in the back somewhere in West Virginia and woke up at the ocean. We had been driving while we slept. The world had reorganized itself around us. I climbed out of the car barefoot onto warm asphalt with the smell of salt in my nose, and the gulls were calling, and my father had his hands on his hips and a smile on his face, and I understood, dimly, that this was what fathers did: they got you to oceans.

On the way home we were always quieter, sunburned and tired, our suitcases full of sandy clothes and shells wrapped in motel towels. I would press my forehead against the window and watch the country roll backward, and the same towns we had cheered through coming would now slip past unremarked, and I would feel the small grief that comes at the end of any good thing, and I would not have known to call it that.

The gym had been transformed by paper streamers and the careful work of a committee that included people I had crushes on. The basketball hoops were folded against the ceiling, the floor was waxed to a high gloss, and a disco ball hung from the rafters throwing slow constellations across the walls. I stood against the wall in a borrowed tie and tried to look like I belonged, and somehow, eventually, I did.

The slow songs were the whole point of the evening, the four minutes during which it might happen, whatever it was. I remember the moment of asking, the long walk across the gym floor that felt like a march, the impossible kindness of a yes. Her hand on my shoulder weighed nothing and weighed everything. I have danced at many weddings since, and none of those dances have changed the world the way one school-gym dance once did.

The chaperones stood at the perimeter in their wool blazers, drinking punch and trying to look bored, but you could tell they were enjoying it secretly, remembering their own dances thirty years gone. The DJ played the same songs every year, songs we knew were corny but loved anyway because everyone in the room knew them too. The corniness was the point. It was the shared language.

After the dance we drove out to the lake in a borrowed car with the windows down and the radio loud and our dress shoes off, and we sat on the hood of the car watching the moon on the water and saying nothing because we didn't yet have the words for what we were feeling. We were seventeen and beautiful and didn't know it, and I would not have known to be grateful, and I am grateful now for all of us.

My corsage was kept in the refrigerator for a week afterward, the petals slowly browning at the edges, before my mother finally threw it out without telling me. I noticed it was gone and didn't say anything either. Some things should not be discussed. The memory of the corsage was more durable than the corsage, and we all knew it, and we let the flowers go without ceremony so the memory could keep.

The bathrooms during a dance were their own small ecosystem, girls fixing hair and consoling each other and reapplying lip gloss, boys hiding from the social pressure of the actual gym, gossip moving between the stalls like a small weather system. I went in once to wash sweat off my hands and came out with three new pieces of information about my class. The bathrooms were almost more interesting than the dancing.

The photographer set up in the hallway near the trophy case with a backdrop of cardboard stars, and we lined up in awkward couples to have our pictures taken. I still have mine in a drawer somewhere, a small square print of two seventeen-year-olds attempting the dignity of grown-ups, doing better than I would have predicted, doing worse than they thought.

At the end of the night the lights came up and the gym became, suddenly and brutally, a gym again, with all its scuffed floors and harsh fluorescent honesty. The magic could not survive that light, and we all knew it, and we filed out into the parking lot half-laughing and half-mourning, knowing we had just lived through something we would always remember and not yet knowing why.

I drove my date home in my father's Buick and we sat in her driveway for a long time not quite saying goodnight, the engine running and the heat blowing and a song neither of us liked playing on the radio. I think back to that driveway often. We were on the edge of so many things, and we sensed it, and we did not know which one to step into first, and so we sat.

The morning after a dance the gym was already restored, the streamers in a trash bag and the basketball hoops back down and the floor scuffed with hundreds of small scuff marks no one would ever account for. I walked into PE that Monday and looked up at the rafters where the disco ball had been, and there was nothing there, and I felt the first small intimation that all evenings end this way, in the unrecognizable plainness of Monday.

The first snow always came overnight, and you knew it before you opened your eyes by the particular quality of the quiet. The light through the curtains was different, brighter and softer at once, and the world outside had been muffled into a hush. I would stand at the window in my pajamas and look at the white untouched lawn and feel a kind of reverence that has not been available to me about anything since.

My mother would have the radio on in the kitchen, listening for school closings, and we would gather around it in our pajamas with held breath. The announcer read the list in alphabetical order, and the waiting was nearly unbearable, and when our school was finally called my brother and I would erupt as though we had won something enormous. We had, in fact, won something enormous.

The snow had a particular smell, sharp and clean and a little metallic, that filled the front hall every time someone came in. The boots went onto a mat by the door and the wet wool of mittens steamed on the radiator. My grandmother would make cocoa with milk on the stove and stir it slowly with a wooden spoon, and the kitchen would smell like chocolate and wet wool together, and that was winter to me, and still is.

We made angels in the front yard, lying back into the cold powder with our arms and legs outstretched, and getting up carefully so as not to disturb the print. Then we would walk back to the porch and turn around and admire our work, and the angels would stay until the next snow fell over them. I have not made a snow angel in twenty years. I do not remember deciding to stop.

The plow would come down our street in the dim early hours, scraping and grumbling and throwing up a wave of snow into the curb that became, by morning, a small mountain range. We would climb it in our snowsuits and dig caves into it and sit inside the caves eating handfuls of fresh snow and feeling like explorers. There has been no kingdom since that has belonged so completely to me.

Inside, the house was warm and dim and smelled of coffee and toast and woodsmoke from the small fire my father had started in the den. The radiators clanked. The dog slept stretched out in front of the heat vent. The snow continued outside, and we knew it would continue, and we knew there was nowhere we had to be, and the day stretched out before us like an enormous gift we did not yet know how to open.

My father would shovel the walk with deliberate slowness, the breath coming out of his mouth in small white clouds, and he would stop now and then to lean on the shovel and look up at the sky as though checking on something. I would watch him from the upstairs window, and even then I think I knew that I was watching something I would want, later, to remember exactly.

The sled we had was wooden with red painted runners and a length of rope tied through two holes in the front. It belonged to my father from his childhood. The wood was nicked and scratched in places he had nicked and scratched it. I pulled it behind me up the hill at the end of the street and rode it down a hundred times every snow day of my childhood, and it now lives in my own attic, waiting.

The trees in the front yard would be heavy with snow and would let go their loads in soft thumps all morning long, and a small avalanche would come down past the kitchen window every few minutes, and you would look up from your cocoa and see it and feel for an instant as though the world were a very kind and inventive place. I think the world was, in fact, a kinder place. Or perhaps I was a kinder version of myself.

We came in at lunch with red cheeks and wet jeans and snow in our hair and the dog with snow in his fur, and my mother would have grilled cheese sandwiches and tomato soup waiting on the table, and the kitchen was the warmest place in the world, and I sat in it understanding nothing about what I had and everything about what I felt.

He came home in a cardboard box in the back of the station wagon when I was seven, a small black puppy with one white paw, and we all sat on the kitchen floor while he turned in confused circles and finally curled up in my brother's lap and slept. We promised many things that day. He would live with us for fourteen years. He kept all his promises. I am not sure we kept ours.

He slept at the foot of my bed every night of his life, the weight of him a small reassurance against my ankles, and I would wake to find him curled exactly where he had been when I fell asleep, as though he had simply held vigil. I learned what it was to be loved with that unwavering, unembarrassed steadiness from him before I knew it from anyone else.

His leash hung on a hook by the back door, and the sound of it being lifted off the hook was the most thrilling sound of his day, and possibly of mine. He would dance and skid on the linoleum and wag his entire body. We walked every evening at six, around the same three blocks, year after year, and he knew every smell on every fence post the way a man knows the names of streets in his own town.

When I came home from school he was waiting at the front window, his face pressed against the glass, and I could see him from the bus stop a block away. He would explode out of the front door when my mother opened it, and would meet me halfway up the walk, and would carry on as though I had returned from a war. I have never since been welcomed home like that.

He had a favorite tennis ball that had been a tennis ball when he found it and was, by the end, a small dense gray sphere of fur and old saliva that we could not throw out without breaking his heart. He would bring it to me and drop it at my feet, and I would hold it gingerly between two fingers and toss it, and he would chase it as though it were the first ball ever invented.

In his last years he could not climb the stairs anymore, and I would carry him up at night and he would settle into his bed beside mine with a long sigh, and I would lie in the dark listening to his breathing and trying to memorize the sound of it because I could feel, even then, that I was running out of time to memorize it. He died on a Tuesday. I still listen for the breathing.

He swam in the lake at my grandmother's cabin every summer, paddling out after sticks I threw, his ears trailing in the water like small flags. The whole dock smelled of wet dog by August. He would shake himself off on my legs and look up at me as though to confirm that this was the best afternoon either of us had ever had, and he was usually right.

He was not a smart dog. He was a profoundly, gloriously average dog, and I loved him without reservation, and the lessons he taught me had nothing to do with intelligence. He taught me about returning. He taught me about pleasure in small things. He taught me that the world is more or less worth getting up for, and that if you greet each morning as though it were the morning, the morning will mostly oblige.

My mother kept his collar in a kitchen drawer for years after he died, and I would come across it occasionally when I was looking for the tape, and I would pick it up and the tags would jingle, and the whole house would be smaller for a moment, and I would put it back and shut the drawer carefully and go on with whatever I had been doing.

There is a worn patch on the carpet at the foot of the bed in my parents' guest room where he used to sleep, and twenty years later you can still see exactly where his body fit. My mother has not replaced the carpet, though she has replaced everything else in that room, and she has not said why, and I have not asked, and we both know.

The library opened at nine and we were sometimes the first ones there, my mother and I, standing on the steps in the cold while the librarian fumbled with her keys on the other side of the glass doors. The smell hit me as soon as we walked in, the particular smell of paper and old paste and the small dust of a thousand bindings settling into themselves.

The children's section had a green carpet shaped like an island and bean bags shaped like frogs, and I would sit on a frog with a stack of picture books beside me and turn the pages slowly, careful not to bend the corners. The librarian whispered when she walked past us, and she always knew exactly which book I would like next, and she would slip it onto the table beside me without saying anything.

There was a card catalog in the lobby that I was allowed to use even though I was too small to reach the upper drawers, and I would pull out the heavy oak drawers and stand on tiptoe and read the typed cards, learning the Dewey decimal system the way other kids were learning baseball stats. I loved that the books had addresses. I miss the drawers.

The chairs in the reading room had leather seats that had grown soft with thirty years of readers, and the lamps on the tables had green glass shades, and the wood was scarred with the careful indifference of a place that knows it is loved. I would pick a chair and pull a book down from the shelf and read for the entire morning without moving, and my mother would find me there at noon.

The check-out desk had a date stamp that the librarian thumped down with a satisfying punch into the back of each book, and the slip of paper had all the previous dates above it, going back years, a small genealogy of borrowers. The stamp was the moment a book briefly became yours, and I loved that moment fiercely.

There was a globe on a wooden stand in the corner of the reference room, and I would spin it slowly and put my finger down at random and read out the name of the country I had landed in, and I would go find a book about that country. I traveled the world from a wooden chair in a library on Saturday mornings. The globe was enough.

The microfilm machine in the back of the library was a great gray contraption that whirred and clattered, and the librarian let me use it once when I was old enough, and I scrolled through newspapers from the year of my birth, the headlines flickering past, and I understood for the first time that the world had been going on before I arrived.

I have driven past that library many times in adulthood, and it is still there, mostly, though they renovated the lobby and removed the card catalog and replaced the green-shaded lamps with overhead fluorescents. I have not gone in. I know what I would find, and I know what I would not, and I prefer the memory.

On rainy Saturdays the library would fill up with people taking shelter, and the place would have a humming, contented atmosphere, like a great public living room. Old men slept in the reading chairs. Mothers read aloud to small children in the corners. The radiator clanked. The rain pattered on the high windows. I belonged there with everyone else, anonymously and completely.

The librarian retired when I was in college, and my mother sent me the clipping from the local paper, a photo of her at the desk smiling shyly under the headline of forty years of service. I cried in my dorm room over a woman I had not seen in eight years. I had not known how much of my childhood she had quietly been holding for me.

We were not allowed downstairs until my parents called us, but we would sit on the top step in the cold dim hallway in our pajamas, waiting, hearing the percolator and the radio and the small productions of grown-up readiness below. My brother and I would whisper guesses about what was under the tree. The minutes lasted hours. They were among the most exquisite minutes of my life.

The tree my father cut down himself every year was always slightly too big for the living room, and the top inch had to be sawed off in the driveway, and we would smell the fresh-cut spruce all day long. The needles got everywhere and stayed until April. The ornaments were a chaos of decades, each one a small biography of the family.

My grandmother's stocking was the one she had knit for herself in 1948, and it hung at the end of the row, slightly smaller than the rest and faded at the cuff. She would empty it slowly on Christmas morning, taking out each small wrapped item and exclaiming over it as though it were the first gift she had ever received, and we would watch her with the patient love of children.

The lights on the tree were the old kind, the big bulbs in red and green and yellow and blue, and when my father plugged them in on Christmas Eve they would buzz faintly and warm the air around the tree, and you could smell the pine needles where the heat touched them. We left a plate of cookies and a glass of milk, and I never quite stopped believing.

My mother insisted that we open one gift each at a time, in turn, so that everyone could see, and the morning would take three hours and the floor would be a sea of wrapping paper and ribbon and the dog would have eaten a bow and the cat would be inside the empty box. I rolled my eyes at the slowness then. I would give anything for a three-hour Christmas morning now.

The smell of bacon would start in the kitchen around ten, and my father would emerge from the living room and put on his apron and make breakfast while my brother and I assembled whatever toy required assembling, the carpet covered in little plastic instructions and small unaccounted-for screws. There was a particular pleasure in eating Christmas breakfast in your pajamas at eleven in the morning.

There was always one gift that my mother had spent the most thought on, the one that meant the most to her, and you could tell which one it was by the way she watched you open it. She would hold her breath. I learned to slow down for those gifts, to read the card carefully, to admire the wrapping, to receive the gift the way she wanted it received.

My grandfather was the only one who would call on Christmas morning, from his apartment in Florida, and he would talk to each of us in turn, and his voice would be a little gruff and a little choked, and he would always end the call the same way: be good, son. He died in March of the next year. I think about that call every December.

By late afternoon the wrapping paper had been bagged and the new toys had been played with and abandoned in favor of the boxes they came in, and the living room had settled into a particular quiet that I associate only with that day. My father would put on a record. My mother would doze on the couch. The tree would still be lit.

I have hosted Christmases of my own now, in my own house, with my own children, and they are wonderful in their own way, and they will be the Christmases my children remember. But I sometimes sit alone in my living room after everyone has gone to bed, looking at the tree, and I find that I am missing my parents' living room with a particular and bottomless gentleness.

The cabin had no key. It had never had a key. You pushed the door open and stepped onto the worn pine floor and the smell of cedar and old fishing tackle met you like an old friend. The screened porch wrapped around two sides, and the screens were dotted with mosquitoes and the husks of moths from previous summers. Nothing about the cabin changed from year to year, and that was the entire point of the cabin.

The dock was three crooked planks balanced on cedar posts driven into the lake bottom by my grandfather in 1962, and they had been replaced piece by piece over the years until almost nothing of the original remained, and yet it was still my grandfather's dock, and everyone on the lake referred to it that way, and the small philosophical implications never bothered any of us.

At night the lake went perfectly still and the loons called from the cove and you could hear someone laughing on a dock half a mile away as clearly as if they were in the next room. We would sit on the porch with citronella candles and listen, and the talk would slow, and the stars would come out one at a time over the trees, and time would do that thing it only did at the lake.

The kitchen had a wood stove we used for cooking and for warmth on cool mornings, and my grandmother kept a coffee pot on it from dawn until dinner. The coffee got progressively stronger throughout the day. By dinnertime it was more like tar. We loved it. I have not tasted coffee like that since, and I do not expect to.

The rowboat lived upturned on the bank, and we would flip it over each morning and bail out the rainwater with a coffee can and row out into the calm of dawn looking for bass. My grandfather would not speak for the whole hour. He would just row and watch the water and look at me occasionally with a small grave nod, and I learned from those silences more than from anything he ever said.

There was a long stretch of afternoon when the heat would push everyone indoors, and the cabin would be very still, and my grandmother would sit at the kitchen table with a crossword and my mother would nap on the screened porch and I would lie on the cool floor of the loft reading a book and listening to the lake lap softly at the dock, and the world would simply pause for a few hours.

We had a swing on the big maple by the water, hung with rope that my grandfather had replaced once in 1981 and never again, the wood worn shiny by decades of bare summer legs. I swung over the lake hundreds of times and never tired of it. The view of the cabin from the top of the swing's arc, framed by leaves and roof and sky, is one of the few images I am certain I will carry with me to the end.

Rain on the tin roof of the cabin was the best sound in the world, a steady percussive comfort that made the inside of the cabin feel like a sealed lantern in the middle of the woods. We would sit at the kitchen table and play gin rummy and listen to the rain, and there was nowhere else to go, and that was the whole pleasure of it: there was nowhere else to go.

My grandfather taught me to fillet a fish on a board nailed to a stump beside the dock, and the blood ran down into the moss and the gulls watched from the shore, and the whole process was, somehow, a small ceremony of belonging to a place. The board is still there, weathered gray. I went back last year. The board remembered me. It is one of the few things that does.

The last morning of our last summer there, before my grandparents sold the place, I went down to the dock alone at dawn and sat with my feet in the water and listened to the loons and tried to memorize everything: the angle of the light, the smell of the pines, the small slap of the water against the planks. I have used that memory often, in many rooms, in many cities. It has not failed me yet.

We woke up before our parents on Saturdays and tiptoed downstairs in our pajamas, and the house was that particular quiet that belonged only to us. The TV came on with a small static pop and a wash of blue light, and we lay on the carpet six inches from the screen with bowls of cereal balanced on our stomachs and watched the cartoons for three uninterrupted hours.

The commercials were as important as the shows: little boys grinning at improbable cereals, little girls in pink rooms with dolls that promised to be your best friend. I learned, on those mornings, the entire taxonomy of toys I would never own and snacks I could not pronounce. The wanting was its own kind of pleasure, separate from the having and possibly better.

The cereal bowls had cartoon characters on the bottom that you only saw once you finished, and there was a small, almost religious satisfaction in the moment of revelation when the last bite was eaten and the bowl could be tilted to show the prize. The milk turned colors. The spoon was almost too sticky to lift. I miss being the kind of person for whom these things were the high points of the morning.

My brother and I had an agreement: I controlled the dial for the first hour, he controlled it for the second, and the third hour we negotiated. The negotiations were intense and sometimes violent. We had a strict moral economy of who had given up what last week. I have not lived inside a moral system that elaborate or that important since.

The reception was bad. We had rabbit-ear antennas with aluminum foil twisted around the ends, and one of us would have to stand holding them at a specific angle for the picture to come in. We took turns. Standing-the-antenna was a small heroic duty, and the standee got to choose the next show, and the system was elaborate and fair, and we administered it gravely.

Our father would come down around nine in his bathrobe with a cup of coffee and look at the screen for a moment without comprehension and then go to the kitchen. He never sat with us. The cartoons were ours. The cartoons were not for fathers. I think of him now, padding past us in his slippers, and I want to call him over and have him sit down beside us on the carpet for once.

There was a special pleasure in the moment the last cartoon ended and the dreaded local programming began, because that meant we had used the morning fully, and the rest of the Saturday lay ahead, and we had been served. We turned off the TV with regret and stretched out on the carpet and looked at the ceiling and felt like small kings of a small kingdom whose entire boundary was the living room.

I remember the particular slant of Saturday morning light through the picture window, falling across the carpet in a long rectangle of pale gold, the dust spinning in it, the cat moving slowly to lie down inside it. The cartoons played on, and the light moved across the room, and we did not move for hours. It was as still and as content as any time of my life has been.

When my parents finally came downstairs around ten the spell would break, but my mother always brought me a glass of orange juice without asking, and she always set it on the coffee table within my reach, and she did not turn off the TV or ask us to come and eat at the table. She understood the morning's grammar. She did not interfere with it. I think of that grace now and I do not know how to thank her for it.

I have watched, with my own children, the cartoons they prefer, and they are good cartoons, mostly, but I cannot help thinking of those long Saturday hours on the carpet with my brother, and I cannot help wishing for my children some equivalent of that small private kingdom. I am not sure they have it. I am not sure they will need it. But I had it, and I am glad I did.

Her name was Catherine and she sat two rows ahead of me in seventh grade English, and she had a single freckle on the back of her neck that I used to study while Mr. Whitlow lectured about commas. I never spoke to her. She never spoke to me. And yet somehow, for the entire year, my whole interior life was organized around her freckle. I have not loved anyone, since, that abstractly. I have loved better, but not more strangely.

I wrote a poem about her in a notebook I kept hidden under my mattress, and the poem was very bad, and I knew it was very bad, and I did not care, because the writing of it was a kind of prayer that nobody, not even me, was meant to understand. I burned the notebook the summer after eighth grade. I sometimes wish I had not, and sometimes I am glad I did.

I would walk a different way home from school just to pass her house, slowing down at the corner to glance up at the windows on the second floor, never seeing her, never expecting to see her, and feeling somehow that the passing itself was enough. The trees on her block were maples that turned a vivid red in October, and to this day I cannot see a red maple without feeling thirteen for a second.

Her laugh in the cafeteria across three tables of seventh graders was the soundtrack of my entire winter. She laughed loudly and without self-consciousness, with her head thrown back, and the whole cafeteria seemed to brighten around her. I never knew what was funny. I just knew the laugh, and I lived for the laugh, and the laugh was enough.

On Valentine's Day I bought her a card at the drugstore and then sat in my room for two hours trying to write a message and then signed it From a Friend and slipped it into her locker through the vent. She never knew. I never told her. I think about that card sometimes, and the boy who slipped it in, and the absolute terror and tenderness with which he did it. He was so young. I forgive him everything.

Catherine moved away the summer before high school, and I learned about it from her best friend in the produce section of the grocery store, and I went home and lay on my bed for the rest of the afternoon staring at the ceiling. The pain was disproportionate and pure. I did not know yet that this was what loss would feel like, only smaller. I would learn.

I saw her once, fifteen years later, in an airport in Atlanta, and I almost didn't recognize her, and she didn't recognize me at all. She walked past me and the whole seventh grade came back in a single rush, the freckle and the laugh and the card in the locker. I stood at the gate with my coffee getting cold and watched her disappear into the crowd, and I thought: there she goes, again.

I never told anyone about her, not even my closest friends at the time, because to name the feeling would have been to risk its dilution. I carried it alone like a small bird in my chest for that whole year, and I have not carried any feeling so privately since. I sometimes miss that secrecy. There was a dignity to it that adult life has not made room for.

She wore a yellow raincoat in the spring, and the raincoat became, in my mind, indistinguishable from the entire phenomenon of Catherine, so that for years I had a small physiological response to yellow raincoats. I still do, a little, though it is muted now, like a station fading on a long drive. The signal is there. The signal is going.

She was not the love of my life. She was barely even a friend. But she was the first occasion of my having an interior life that was about someone other than me, and for that I owe her a debt I cannot pay, and she does not know I owe it, and I am grateful for the small private kingdom of caring she ushered me into without ever knowing she had.

The bell over the door announced you whenever you came in, and the man behind the counter looked up from his newspaper and nodded, and you nodded back, and that was the entire ceremony of belonging to a neighborhood. The store smelled of penny candy and floor wax and the faint ammonia of the cleaner he used on the counter every morning at six.

He kept the candy in big glass jars on the counter, and you would point at what you wanted and he would unscrew the lid and use a small pair of tongs to drop the candies one by one into a paper sack. The whole transaction was slow, ceremonial, and full of choices. I could spend forty-five cents on a Saturday morning and feel like a person of consequence.

He knew my mother's name and my mother's mother's name, and he kept a tab in a small black notebook behind the counter, and on Fridays my mother would stop in and settle up, and they would talk about the weather and his nephew's wedding for fifteen minutes. There was no efficiency to any of it. There was something else, something that no transaction at a self-checkout has ever once provided.

The Sunday papers were stacked just inside the door, smelling of fresh ink, and on top of them was a tin can with a slot in the lid, and you took a paper and dropped your quarters in and trusted yourself to be trusted. He never counted. He never had to. The neighborhood was a system of small assumed honors, and the can was one of them, and the can held them all.

His wife sat in a chair near the back during the day, peeling potatoes or shelling peas or sometimes simply watching the door, and she would smile at the children who came in and slip them a piece of caramel from her apron pocket. She did not speak much English. She did not need to. The caramel was the language. The smile was the language. I have not been welcomed by any stranger as warmly since.

The store was open at hours that did not exist anywhere else in my life. He opened at six and closed when the last customer left, which was sometimes eleven and sometimes nine and once, during a blizzard, three in the afternoon. There were no posted hours. There was just him, and the door, and the bell, and the small endless rhythm of opening and closing.

His son took over the store in the late nineties, briefly, and tried to modernize it, and it did not last. The son sold the building to a real estate company. It is a coffee chain now, with a chalkboard menu and a logo on the cup. I do not begrudge the new place. I just walk past it on the way home from the train, and I do not look at the windows.

I went to his funeral. The church was packed with people who had been buying milk and lottery tickets and newspaper from him for forty years, and we all stood up when his name was called, and there were hundreds of us, and his wife wept, and his sons read a list of customers who had asked to be mentioned. I had asked to be mentioned. I have asked for very few things in my life so directly.

There was a wooden bench outside the store where old men sat in good weather, and you could pass them at any hour of any day. They smoked and watched the cars and gossiped quietly in three different languages. Sometimes one of them would call me over and give me a piece of gum from a foil-wrapped pack. I did not know any of their names. They were all called Sir to me, and that was correct.

The whole block used to be a kind of village, and the store was the village square, and everything that happened on that block at some point passed through that doorway. Now the village is gone and the square is gone, and the people who knew the names and the small honors have mostly gone too. I am one of the few left who remembers, and I am not sure what to do with the remembering.

Her letters came once a month from a small town in Vermont, and the envelopes had been touched by her hand and crossed three states to reach mine, and I could not have explained, at twelve, why that mattered, but it mattered enormously. I would read each letter standing at the mailbox and then again on the walk back to the house and then a third time in my room with the door closed.

She had careful round handwriting and used a different colored pen for each paragraph, and she drew small flowers in the margins. She told me about her brother and her dog and the snow that came in October that year, and I told her about my school and my band concerts and the cat we had just gotten, and we built between us, by mail, a friendship that had no other body but the paper.

I kept her letters in a shoebox under my bed, tied with a length of yellow ribbon, and I would take them out occasionally and reread them in chronological order, watching our friendship develop on paper across two years. I have not reread them in many years. I do not have to. I remember almost everything she wrote. The brain is strangely loyal to those early correspondences.

The waiting was as important as the receiving. From the moment I sent a letter I would begin to wait for the reply, and the days would stretch, and I would check the mailbox after school every day, and the eventual arrival of the answer was a small and complete joy that arrived only because I had been patient for it. I miss being patient like that. I miss the inefficiency of the friendship.

She sent me a maple leaf pressed in wax paper one autumn, and I kept it in the back of my dictionary, and it is still there, dry as a chip, the color of weak rust. I open the dictionary now and then for some particular word and find the leaf and feel an unaccountable affection for a girl I never met and who has not written to me in thirty years.

We sent each other our school pictures the year we were thirteen, and I taped hers to the inside of my locker, and she taped mine to the inside of hers, and we wrote to each other about how strange it was to know what the other looked like, and the friendship adjusted itself slightly to accommodate the new information, but did not change very much.

The last letter I got from her was after high school graduation, and it was longer than usual, and at the end she wrote that she was going to college in California and would write again when she got settled. She never did. I waited for that letter for nearly two years before I understood that the friendship had simply ended, the way some friendships end, with no announcement and no fault.

I have looked her up online once or twice. She seems to be doing well. She has a husband and two children and a job in a town I have never been to. I have not reached out. I do not want to disturb the version of her that lives in the shoebox under the bed. That version is mine. The one in the world belongs to her.

I wonder sometimes whether she still has my letters. I imagine her shoebox in some closet in some house I have never seen. I imagine her taking out my letters at thirty-five and rereading them and remembering a boy from a town she never visited. I hope she does. I hope at least one of us still keeps the other in a box, ribbon-tied, waiting.

It taught me how to write, in a way that no class did. It taught me that words on paper could carry a person across hundreds of miles and arrive intact in another house and be unfolded by another hand and felt as a small visit. I have written a thousand emails since. None of them have made anyone wait by a mailbox. None of them have been kept in a shoebox under a bed.

The boardwalk lit up at dusk and the carnival lights bled into the wet wood and the salt air, and the whole strip became a long string of colored bulbs reflected in puddles, and the sound of the rides braided with the sound of the gulls and the surf. We walked the length of it slowly, in no hurry, with cotton candy on our fingers and the day still warm on our shoulders.

The Ferris wheel turned slowly against the darkening sky, and from the top you could see the whole town and the whole ocean and the small headlights of cars on the highway going home. We stopped at the very top for a moment when the wheel paused to let someone on below, and we did not speak, and the lights of the town spread out before us, and the wind smelled of salt and grease and fireworks.

The man at the ring-toss had a voice like sandpaper and called out to everyone who passed, and I lost two dollars trying to win a stuffed bear and I would lose two dollars again right now if it would put me back at that booth, with that voice, on that boardwalk, with sand in my shoes and someone holding my hand.

The carousel had horses with chipped paint and glass eyes that no longer quite matched, and I rode it long past the age at which I should have, holding onto the brass pole and watching the lights blur past, and the calliope played a song I have never heard outside of a carousel and that I would recognize instantly if I heard it from a closed window two blocks away.

The funnel cake stand had a line that wrapped around the back, and the powdered sugar got on everything, and we ate the cake out of paper plates with white plastic forks while standing at the rail looking out over the dark water. The sugar stuck to my sister's chin. The salt air pulled the heat out of the cake quickly. We did not say much. We did not have to.

The fortune teller had a small canvas booth strung with Christmas lights, and the woman inside wore many scarves and spoke in a half-whispered voice that I knew at the time was a costume, and yet I sat down across from her and let her tell me about the line of my future, and I have never quite stopped believing some of what she said.

The arcade was at the far end of the boardwalk, and the floor sloped slightly toward the ocean, and the change machines clanked, and the air smelled of metal and stale popcorn, and we put quarters into the skeeball lanes until our pockets were empty and our hands were striped with the brown ink of paper tickets. We never had enough tickets for the good prizes. We took a plastic ring and were satisfied.

Walking back to the car at the end of the night, the carnival's noise receded behind us and the dark of the parking lot closed in, and the bumpy plastic bag I carried was full of small useless things that meant the world. I could feel sand in my socks. I could smell the funnel cake in my hair. I knew I would sleep with my window open and dream of the lights, and I did.

The boardwalk has been rebuilt twice since then, after two different storms, and the carnival operators have changed, and most of the booths I remember are gone. I walked the length of it last summer with my own children, and they were delighted by their own version, and I was glad. But I was also somewhere else for a moment, walking it with my sister thirty years ago, holding her sticky hand.

There was a moment near the end of every visit, walking back through the carnival under all those bulbs, when I would feel a small premonitory grief without knowing what to call it, because I sensed even then that the night was ending and that nights like that one did not repeat themselves, and I tried to walk slower, and the night kept ending anyway, the way nights do.

The cousins arrived in waves through the gate that hadn't been latched all afternoon, and the lawn filled slowly with folding chairs and aunts in summer dresses and uncles in shorts they wore only on this one weekend a year. My grandmother sat at the head of the picnic table like a small queen, and everyone, before doing anything else, went to her chair to kiss her cheek.

There was always too much food. The picnic table groaned with potato salads in three different styles, three Jell-O molds in three competing colors, two competing fried chickens, my Aunt Marge's deviled eggs in a special blue dish she would not lend to anyone, and a watermelon the size of a small dog. Nobody could ever finish, and yet somehow, by sundown, every dish was empty.

The children formed their own small republic at one end of the yard, the cousins reorganizing the alliances they had built and broken at the previous year's reunion, running through the sprinkler my grandfather had set on the lawn. We negotiated who was best friends with whom in a complex annual treaty. The adults at the picnic table laughed and forgot us for whole hours. It was the freest I have ever been.

Uncle Earl always told the same three stories, and we always laughed at the same three places, and his wife always said oh Earl, not the duck story again, and he always told it anyway. The duck story has now outlived Uncle Earl by twelve years. I told it last summer to my own children, and they laughed at the same three places, and I caught myself saying it in his voice.

The horseshoes came out late in the afternoon, and the uncles took it more seriously than was strictly reasonable. There was a small notebook of historical scores. There were rules disputes. There was once a yelling match between my father and his brother in 1987 that ended with my grandmother walking out onto the lawn and ending it with one sentence, and they were boys again, and they went back to throwing.

My grandfather strung up the colored lights every year for the evening, and as the dusk came on he would walk slowly through the yard and turn each strand on with a small click, and the whole yard would brighten softly, and the aunts would say oh, oh, look, and the smaller children would chase each other under the lights with sparklers, and there has been no party since that has had quite that quality.

After dinner the cousins lay on the cool grass on our backs and looked up at the stars and tried to identify the constellations my oldest cousin claimed to know. He didn't actually know. He was making them up. But we believed him, and the constellations he invented are still the constellations I look for when I lie in any backyard at night, all these decades later.

The last hour was always the hardest, the long string of goodbyes, the aunts collecting their dishes, the uncles folding chairs, the cousins making each other promise to write, knowing we wouldn't, or not enough. The cars pulled out of the driveway one by one, and the lights of the lawn dimmed, and my grandmother stood at the gate waving until the last car was out of sight.

The grandparents are gone now, the house has been sold, and we have not held a reunion in nine years. There has been talk, every summer, of organizing one, and someone always volunteers, and somehow it doesn't happen. The family has scattered. The yard belongs to other people now. The colored lights, I imagine, are in a box in someone's attic, and I would like very much to know whose attic.

I have wondered, in the years since, what made those afternoons so durable in memory, and I have decided it was the rare experience of being held in a circle of people who were obligated to love you and mostly chose to, who had known you since before you were yourself, and who would, on this one day each year, make room for you at the table without question or comment.

The workshop smelled of sawdust and motor oil and the particular faint sweet smell of WD-40, and the radio was always on, tuned to the ball game or the talk station, and my father moved through that small kingdom of tools with the slow certainty of a man who knew where every wrench had lived since 1974. I was allowed in, but barely. I learned to stand still and watch.

He had pegboards on the walls with the outlines of every tool drawn in black marker, so that the absence of any tool was immediately visible. He never said a word when I borrowed something. He just looked at the empty outline and waited, and eventually the tool came back, and the empty outline filled again, and the geometry of the workshop was restored.

The workbench was a slab of pine he had built himself in 1971, and the surface was scarred and gouged by fifty years of small careful violences, every scar a story he could probably tell. He would sometimes run his hand across it absently while thinking. The bench was the one piece of furniture in his life that he had made, and it had outlasted everything else he ever owned.

He taught me how to sharpen a pencil with a pocket knife on a Saturday afternoon in November when I was eight, and I have never forgotten the lesson, and the smell of cedar shavings still puts me back on the stool beside his workbench with the small concentrated knit of his eyebrows above the work, and my hand inside his hand, and the slow paring away of the wood.

He kept jars of nails and screws sorted by size on a high shelf, the lids fastened to the underside of the shelf above so that you could unscrew the jar with one hand while the lid stayed in place. I have inherited this system. I cannot pass a jar of mixed screws without wanting to sort them. He left me a small obsession, and I am grateful for it.
