The workshop got cold in winter, and he kept a small electric heater on the floor by the bench, and it glowed orange, and we would huddle near it between tasks, and he would pour us both coffee from the thermos he had carried since the early eighties, and we would not say much, and the coffee was strong, and the morning was the morning, and I was the only other person allowed in the workshop with him on winter Saturdays.

When he died I went out to the workshop alone before any of the relatives arrived, and I stood in the middle of it and breathed in the smell, and I touched the pegboard, and the tools were all in their outlines, and I felt for a moment as though he had just stepped out to get a part and would be back any minute. I waited there a long time. He did not come back. The workshop was kind to me anyway.

I took home a single hammer from the workshop, the wooden-handled one he had used most often, and the head is loose and the handle has been replaced twice, but the grain of the wood is shaped to his palm, and now to mine, and I use it for small jobs around my own house, and each use is a small ceremony I do not announce.

The radio he kept on the shelf is on my workbench now, the same model, plugged in but no longer tuned to anything specific because the station he listened to does not exist anymore. I turn it on sometimes anyway and let the static play, and the static is a comfort I cannot fully explain to anyone who did not grow up beside that particular sound.

I think now that the workshop was where he loved me most directly. He was not a man for embraces or speeches. He was a man who would set a piece of wood in front of you, and a tool in your hand, and stand patiently while you ruined it the first time, and then quietly hand you another piece. That was tenderness. I did not know it at the time. I know it now.

We sat in the cheap seats high up the third base line, and from there the whole field was a green geometry below us, the dust at the bases lifting in small puffs whenever a runner went by, and the lights had a way of coming on right around the seventh inning so that the dusk had to give up its color and the field became a pool of brightness in a darkening sky.

My grandfather brought a transistor radio and listened to the announcer call the same game he was watching, and I asked him once why and he said the announcer saw it better. I have thought about that often since. He believed the language of a thing could improve on the thing. He was probably right. The hot dogs cost a dollar then, and they came in foil, and the foil burned your fingers.

The organ in the old ballpark played between innings, and the man at the keys had a sense of humor that everyone in the park understood, and certain songs always meant certain things, and you learned the language by the third game of the season. The organist died one summer. The replacement was not as good. We all noticed without speaking about it. The park was less of a place after that.

The vendor walking up our aisle with peanuts called out in a voice so practiced it had become an instrument, and you would raise a hand and he would underhand a bag the length of three rows directly into your lap, and the change came back wrapped in the receipt, and the whole transaction had a grace I cannot describe to my children, who have only known concession lines.

I caught a foul ball once when I was nine, a soft pop-up that bounced once on the empty seat in front of me and into my lap, and my grandfather lifted me up onto his shoulders and showed me to the crowd, and the people around us applauded, and I have never felt as much like a hero as I felt that one afternoon. The ball is in a box in my closet. I cannot bring myself to throw it out.

The seventh-inning stretch was the moment everyone stood up and sang together, all those strangers around us suddenly a chorus, and the organist played the song the way it had always been played, and my grandfather sang in his unselfconscious old man's voice, and I held his hand and I sang too, and we were part of a thing larger than the two of us for that one minute.

Driving home after a night game, the radio still on with the postgame show, the streetlights of the city giving way to the streetlights of the suburbs and then the dark of the back roads, my grandfather would sometimes simply hum to himself and I would press my forehead against the window and watch the dark fields slide past, and I would feel that I had been given an evening.

The old ballpark was torn down in 2005 and replaced by a stadium with a glass concourse and craft beer and a scoreboard the size of a movie screen. I have been to the new place. It is nicer in every measurable way. It is not the same place. It will never be the same place. I do not begrudge the new place. I just look at it and think of the old one underneath.

My grandfather kept score in a little ringed book with a pencil, marking each play in the elaborate shorthand he had learned in the army, and at the end of the game he would tear out the page and put it in his jacket pocket. He kept those pages in a shoebox for forty years. I inherited the shoebox. There are thousands of innings in it. There is a small map of his summers.

There was something about the pace of those games that the world has since lost the capacity for, the willingness to sit in one place for three and a half hours and watch slow events unfold, the patience of expecting a beautiful play that might never come and being all right if it didn't. I learned patience at that ballpark. I have not always remembered the lesson, but I learned it.

The path to the swimming hole was a quarter mile down through the pines, the needles soft under bare feet, and you smelled the water before you saw it, the cool damp green smell that meant summer. We came every afternoon after lunch with damp towels around our necks and never once tired of the same five-foot jump off the same flat rock into the same brown-green pool.

There was a rope swing tied to a sycamore that hung over the deepest part, and the rope was always wet, and the wood handle had been worn smooth by a hundred summers of children, and you grabbed it and ran three steps and pushed off and flew for a single suspended second before the water took you. I dream of that second more often than I admit.

The older boys would dare each other into the deepest dive, and they would come up gasping with their hair plastered down and their eyes wide, and we younger ones would watch from the rock and learn what it meant to do something that was a little dangerous and to be praised for it. We were small students of bravery. We graduated, mostly, into bigger studies.

The minnows came up to your ankles in the shallows if you stood very still, the smallest possible silver flashes, like a thought you could not quite hold onto. I would stand for whole minutes with my toes in the silt watching them. My mother used to call from the bank to ask what I was doing, and I would say nothing, and that was the truthful answer and also the most important answer.

There was a flat shelf of stone on the east bank where we ate our sandwiches, the bread already a little damp from being wrapped in waxed paper in a hot tin lunchbox, and the chips were always a little soft, and the juice in the jar was warm, and it was the best lunch of my life, eaten on a rock with wet hair, with the sun on my shoulders and my friends arguing about something pointless.

On the hottest days the older kids' fathers would come down too after work, in their undershirts, carrying cans of beer in a paper sack, and they would sit on the bank in folding chairs and watch us swim and not say very much, and I remember thinking how strange it was that men I never saw without ties were now barefoot in the leaves, and I think I understood for the first time that adults had also been children.

The water in late August always carried the first chill of the coming fall, and you knew, swimming in it, that the summer was beginning to end, and you swam harder in protest, and the cold rose up your legs anyway, and you got out and stood shivering on the rock and the next year of school began to take shape in your mind whether you wanted it to or not.

The county fenced off the swimming hole in 1997 for liability reasons after the timber company that owned the land changed hands. The sign reads No Trespassing in bright yellow. I have walked down the path twice in twenty years to see the fence, and each time I have stood there for a long minute and listened to the water through the trees, and I have not climbed the fence, and I have walked back up.

I have brought my own children to swim in nice lakes and clean pools, and they enjoy themselves, and I am glad they have what they have. But I have not yet been able to find them a swimming hole. I am not sure swimming holes still exist in the way they did. I am not sure the children of this generation know what to do with a place that nobody owns and that has no lifeguard.

Sometimes when I am drifting off to sleep I am back on the rope swing, mid-arc, the moment before the water, the moment of pure unaccountable freedom, the wind on my chest, my hands tight on the wet wood, the day still warm, the whole summer still ahead, and my mother somewhere on the bank, and the world hung in a long breath that has not yet decided to end.

The chalkboards in the elementary school were that particular soft green, and the chalk left a small white cloud whenever you wrote, and the teacher's chalk smelled different from the regular chalk, and I would inhale near the tray on my way back from the pencil sharpener. The eraser bins had a felt-soft thud when you set the erasers down. The whole room smelled, faintly and forever, of dust and rubber and warm radiator.

It was a privilege to be chosen to clap the erasers after school, and you were chosen by some private logic of the teacher that you spent the day trying to deserve. Two erasers in each hand, you went outside behind the building and clapped them together, and the chalk dust hung in the air in pale clouds and settled on your shoes and your hair, and I remember walking back inside marked by the small honor.

The squeak of the chalk against the board was a sound that could fill a quiet classroom with a small electrical excitement, the squeak that made everyone wince and then smile, the squeak that was always followed by Mrs. Albright apologizing and tilting the chalk slightly. She held the chalk between her ring and middle fingers, the way old smokers hold cigarettes. The classroom is gone. Her hand is gone. The squeak is in me.

The board at the front had a pull-down map of the world, faded and water-stained, with countries on it that no longer existed by the time I learned the names. I traced the borders with my eyes during math class. I gave myself secret journeys. I went to East Germany on a Tuesday in March and to Yugoslavia on a Wednesday, and those countries are not on any map I can find now, but they are on the one in my head.

There was a small box of colored chalk in the cabinet that came out only for special projects, and the colors were never quite right against the green: the red looked pink, the yellow looked thin, the blue was almost white. We loved them anyway, because they meant something special was happening. I have not used colored chalk in thirty-five years. I would know one in the dark.

The teacher kept the names of students who had misbehaved on the right edge of the board, in a small column, and each name was a small public shame, and there was a particular relief at the end of the day when she walked the eraser down that column and erased the names back into anonymity. I had my name up there twice. I remember the erasing more clearly than the writing.

The first morning of school each year the board was washed perfectly clean, a smooth dark green expanse, and Mrs. Albright would write her name in the upper left corner in her round generous hand, and underneath she would write the date, and the year would officially begin. I cannot see a clean chalkboard now without expecting the year to begin.

When they renovated the school in the late nineties they replaced all the chalkboards with whiteboards, and the chalk dust that had hung in the air for sixty years finally settled. I went back as an alumnus and saw the new boards and felt a small disorientation, as though the school had agreed to forget itself. The whiteboards are more efficient. They will not, however, ever be missed.

I keep a small piece of chalk in a drawer in my office now, for no reason I can fully justify. I take it out occasionally and roll it between my fingers and smell the dust on my hands afterward, and the entire third-grade classroom returns: the radiator, Mrs. Albright's perfume, the squeak, the small chalk-white halo around her sleeve at the end of every day.

I think now that the chalkboard was a kind of contract between the teacher and the room, the promise that whatever was written there mattered for the day and would be erased by night, that learning was provisional and renewable and not a permanent burden. The whiteboard has none of that grammar. The whiteboard pretends that knowledge is clean. The chalkboard knew it was dusty.

We arrived an hour before sunset and parked on the long grassy slope and pointed the car at the screen and waited for the dark, eating the food my mother had packed in a paper sack because the concession stand was too expensive. The screen looked enormous against the orange sky, and the speakers hung from poles by the cars, and the air smelled of summer grass and engine heat and someone's grill in the next row.

My brother and I lay on the hood of the car with our backs against the windshield, looking up at the screen and at the stars beginning to come out beside it, and the speaker by my father's window crackled the opening music of the cartoon. There was nowhere in the world we would rather have been, and we did not know we were lucky, and that is the particular blessing of being a child at a drive-in.

The intermission cartoon advertised the snack bar, the dancing hot dog and the singing soda cup parading across the screen, and my mother would reach into the back seat and pass us each a soft warm soda and a homemade brownie wrapped in waxed paper, and the dancing hot dog could not have improved on what we had. I have not seen a dancing hot dog since. I miss him, in a way.

By the second movie my brother was asleep with his head in my lap, and I was half asleep myself, and my parents sat in the front seat quietly holding hands, and the light from the screen flickered across all of us, and I think now that I was being given a portrait of marriage I would not understand for thirty years. I keep that portrait still. It is one of the things by which I know what to look for.

The drive home was the best part. The road was empty, and the radio played softly, and the cool night air came in the open windows, and my mother turned around occasionally to look at us asleep in the back and adjust the blanket. I sometimes pretended to be asleep just to be looked at like that. I sometimes still pretend to be asleep, in a manner of speaking. I miss being looked at like that.

The screen out at the edge of town was held up by an enormous wooden frame, and on hot afternoons before the show you could see the screen shimmer slightly in the heat. The asphalt of the lot held the day's warmth long into the evening. Couples in the back rows steamed up their windows. We pretended not to notice. We were children, and we noticed everything, and we kept what we noticed private.

The drive-in closed in 1993, and the screen stood for almost a decade afterward, gradually peeling and blackening at the corners, a vast blank face looking out over what had become a parking lot for a tractor dealership. They tore it down eventually. I drove past the day after. There was just a flat empty patch where it had been. The sky behind it had no edge.

I have been to one of the few drive-ins still operating, on a road trip out west, and the experience was very nearly the same, and yet something about it felt like a costume of itself. The hot dogs were too good. The audio came through your car stereo. The teenagers running the booth knew exactly what they were preserving. Nostalgia, when you can buy a ticket to it, is not quite the same animal.

There was a moment late in every drive-in evening when the second feature was rolling and most of the cars had quieted down and the night was deep and cool, and you could hear the night insects under the sound of the movie, and the air smelled of someone's cigarettes carried over from two rows up, and the whole experience was so unrepeatable that I find myself, decades later, simply sitting and remembering the smell of it.

We left after the second feature with the rest of the cars in a slow patient line, our headlights coming on one by one in the dim lot, the speakers swinging gently on their poles as we drove past, and the gravel crunching under the tires, and the long quiet exit toward the highway, and I remember thinking, even at ten, that nights this good probably did not happen to everyone, and I was right.

We walked the same route every afternoon: down her street, around the duck pond, past the old church with the green doors, and back. The walk took thirty-eight minutes and we both knew it took thirty-eight minutes, and we did not walk faster or slower than we ever had. She held my hand the whole way until I was probably too old for it, and she stopped only when I stopped, which was not for a long time.

She named every flower we passed, in English and sometimes in the German she only used for plants and small private exclamations, and I learned by repetition the names of irises and hollyhocks and asters, and I knew without being told that names mattered, that to know a thing's name was a kind of attentiveness, that the world rewarded the people who bothered to ask what it was called.

There was a bench by the duck pond where we always rested, and she would unwrap a piece of stale bread from her handkerchief and we would toss the bread to the ducks, and the ducks would race for the pieces, and she would laugh quietly at the small commotion she had caused. The bench is still there. The pond is still there. The ducks are not, presumably, the same ducks. The bread is no longer brought.

She walked slowly, and I learned to walk slowly with her, and I think now that this is the most important skill she taught me, more important than any of the plant names. I walk too fast in my own life. She would notice. She would put her hand on my forearm and say something like there is no hurry, my dear, the world will still be there. The world has, so far, still been there.

We stopped at the same bakery on the way home every Friday, and she bought me a small almond cookie and herself a slice of poppy seed cake, and we ate them on the walk and I would have crumbs on my chin all afternoon. The bakery closed when I was in high school. The space is a tax office now. I have never managed to find an almond cookie that tastes the way that one did, and I have stopped looking.

She talked, on those walks, about things she did not talk about anywhere else: about her sister who had died young, about the boat across, about the first apartment she shared with my grandfather and how cold it was. The walks were her way of giving me her life slowly, piece by piece, in installments she paid out at the speed of her footsteps, and I received them without knowing I was receiving anything.

On the last walk we took together, when she was already not quite herself, she stopped at the duck pond and looked at it for a long time without speaking, and then she said it had been here when she was a girl, and I had not known that, and I felt the whole of her life suddenly anchored to that small green water. I think of that pond differently now. I think of it as hers.

After she died I walked the route alone one afternoon, the whole thirty-eight minutes, and I named the flowers as I passed them, and I sat on the bench by the pond, and I went into the bakery's replacement and ordered a coffee I did not want, and I cried at one specific bend in the path that I cannot now even locate on a map. The route is a small holy thing now. I have not walked it since.

I sometimes walk in my own neighborhood at her pace deliberately, like a small private discipline, and I name the trees I pass, and I do not check my phone, and I let the walk take the time it takes, and the walk is a small reconstruction of her, and she would not have known to be proud of me, but she would have been.

There was a small joke between us, on those walks, that the duck with the white feather on its head was the king and we were obligated to bow. I have not bowed to a duck in many years. I have not, since, met a duck that I felt was a king. I think probably the king is dead. Long live the king.

subtopic: evening news on a console TV
sentence: The console TV in the living room was a piece of furniture as much as an appliance, a long mahogany cabinet on small wooden legs, with the screen set into the front and a row of knobs along the bottom. My father turned it on every night at six-thirty with a satisfying mechanical click and a low warming hum, and the anchorman's face slowly rose into focus from a gray void.

subtopic: evening news on a console TV
sentence: The anchorman wore a sober gray suit and a perfectly knotted tie and read the news without smiling and without interrupting himself, and somehow, in his solemn unbroken voice, the world arrived in our living room each evening at six-thirty, organized and accounted for. I trusted him. I think the whole country trusted him. I do not know that we trust anyone in quite that way anymore.

subtopic: evening news on a console TV
sentence: My mother brought my father a small bowl of peanuts on a TV tray, and he would eat them slowly while watching the news, and I would sit on the carpet at his feet and watch with him, understanding very little of what was being reported. The names of cities, the columns of dust, the helicopters, the men in uniform. The world was being given to me in small pieces I would only later assemble.

subtopic: evening news on a console TV
sentence: When the weatherman came on my father always sat forward slightly. He had been a farmer's son. He took the weather seriously, the way you take the weather seriously when it has shaped the year of your boyhood. The weatherman had a small wooden pointer that he tapped against the map, and the map had snowflakes and sun symbols and small smiling clouds, and I learned the names of fronts and the meaning of pressure.

subtopic: evening news on a console TV
sentence: At the end of the news there was always a small human-interest story, the duck that had found its way to the school, the man who had saved a stranger, the local centenarian, and the anchorman would smile slightly at the camera as he read it, and the music would come up, and the day would end. I have not watched a piece of news end with a smile like that in many years.

subtopic: evening news on a console TV
sentence: The reception on the rabbit ears was sometimes bad and the picture would dissolve into a grainy snow, and my father would adjust the antennas with one hand while keeping his eyes on the screen, and somehow he always found the angle that brought the anchorman back into focus. The geometry of his hand was the geometry of the news in our house. He passed it down by example, and I learned it without lessons.

subtopic: evening news on a console TV
sentence: After the news, the console television was turned off with another satisfying click, and the picture collapsed inward to a single bright dot at the center of the screen, and the dot lingered for a moment as if reluctant, and then went black. I would sometimes stay in the room a moment longer just to watch the dot fade. The dot was a small ceremony of conclusion. The dot does not exist on modern televisions. I miss it.

subtopic: evening news on a console TV
sentence: The anchorman died in 2009. He had retired years before, but I remember reading the news of his death in the paper and feeling a particular orphaned feeling, as though some last piece of my father's living room had been finally taken down and packed away. My father had been dead for six years. The two losses became, in my head, a single loss, and the loss is of an evening at six-thirty.

subtopic: evening news on a console TV
sentence: The console television was given to a younger cousin when my parents downsized. It still worked. I do not know what became of it after that. I sometimes imagine it in an attic somewhere, the cabinet still polished, the picture still capable of focusing, waiting for someone to turn the knob at six-thirty and bring back the news. There would be no news to bring back. But the dot would still glow, and that would be enough.

subtopic: evening news on a console TV
sentence: What I miss about that television, I think, is the agreement it represented: that at six-thirty the family stopped what it was doing and gathered to be informed together, in one room, from one trusted voice, with no scrolling commentary at the bottom. The world was complicated then too. But the ritual implied it could be made sense of, briefly, by sitting together and listening, and the implication itself was a kind of comfort.

Rainy Sunday afternoons were the slowest hours of the week, and in our house they had a sacred quality. My mother put on a kettle and made tea, my father lay on the couch with the paper, my brother and I sprawled on the carpet with our books and our coloring and the dog asleep between us. The rain on the windows was steady. Nobody was expected anywhere. The whole house held still.

There was a particular smell that arrived in our living room on rainy Sundays, a small blend of warm dust and damp wood and the cinnamon something my mother always seemed to be baking, and the smell was so specific to that one weather and that one room that I sometimes find myself searching for it in other rainy houses, and it is never quite there, and I am always disappointed, and yet I keep searching.

My father read the Sunday paper section by section in a particular order: news first, then editorials, then sports, then the comics last, and he would pass each section over to my mother as he finished it without looking up, and she would catch it without looking up, and the choreography had been worked out somewhere in the seventies and never altered.

I would read for hours in the corner armchair, with my legs over the armrest, looking up only when the kettle whistled or when the dog stirred to change positions. The light in the room was dim and gray-green and somehow encouraging, the kind of light that made reading feel like the most important thing in the world. I do not read like that anymore. I do not know how to.

We would make popcorn on the stove in a big pot, and the kernels would crackle against the lid, and the whole kitchen would smell of hot oil and salt, and my mother would dump it into the big yellow bowl and sprinkle it with butter, and we would carry the bowl back to the living room and pass it around. The bowl always emptied. There was always more popcorn. It was a small system of abundance.

Sometimes my father would put on a record, very quiet, just a presence under the rain, something instrumental and old, and the music would mix with the weather, and I think that mix was the soundtrack of my entire childhood. I have not, since, found music that fits so completely with rain. I have not, since, sat through a rain like that one without somewhere to be.

By late afternoon the rain would let up slightly and the light would change, and the dog would lift his head and look at the door hopefully, and my father would yawn and stretch and put down the paper and say well, and that one syllable was the signal that the afternoon had ended and life would gradually resume. I dreaded the well. I waited for the well to come and waited for it to be postponed.

I tried, when I had my own house, to recreate that afternoon. I made tea. I put on quiet music. I lay on the couch with a book. The rain came down outside. It was almost the same, and yet it was not the same, and the missing piece was the family. The afternoon was not the afternoon without the bodies of the people I loved in their habitual positions around the room.

It rained two weeks ago, a long slow Sunday rain that came on around eleven and didn't let up until five, and I sat in my own living room with my own tea and thought of all of them, my parents and my brother and the dog, and I closed my eyes, and for a long unbroken moment, I was there again, with no effort, as if the room had simply opened up around me.

What I think now is that those afternoons taught me, before I knew I was being taught, that pleasure was sometimes the absence of activity, that the most precious hours of a life might be the ones in which absolutely nothing happens, in which the family is simply together in their own attentions, in which the rain is the only voice and the room is the entire world.

I still remember the smell of the cabins at Camp Wabanaki, that particular mix of pine sap and lake water and the cedar shavings they put down on the floor every June. We slept in bunks with thin mattresses and complained about everything and I would give almost anything to be back there now, lacing up wet sneakers at six in the morning to walk down to the dock for the polar bear swim.

The dining hall had screen doors that slammed in a rhythm I can still hear, and we wrote our names on the rafters in pencil because the counselors looked the other way. My name is probably still up there, faint and crooked, with a heart drawn around it by a boy whose face I cannot quite remember anymore.

Color war week was the most serious thing I had ever been part of, and I cried genuine tears the year the blue team lost the canoe race because of a tipped paddle. I find myself missing that level of feeling, when the outcome of a tug-of-war on a dewy field at dusk could feel like the most consequential event of the entire summer.

There was a song they made us sing every night by the campfire, something about silver moons and friendships that would never end, and at the time I thought it was corny. I would sing it now, in the dark, alone in my kitchen, if I could remember all the words.

We tied friendship bracelets onto each other's wrists on the last day and swore we would write, and we did, for a while, in handwriting that grew tidier and more distant each year. The bracelets eventually frayed off in the shower one by one, and so did the friendships, and only the memory remains, gilded.

The lake had a raft anchored about fifty yards from shore, and earning the right to swim out to it felt like a rite of passage. I remember the cold board under my back when I finally made it, and how the sky looked from there, and how my older sister waved from the dock like I had become someone new.

Our counselor was a college sophomore named Sarah who seemed impossibly grown up to me at twelve, and she let us braid her hair and ask her questions about boys. I think of her sometimes and hope she is well, and hope she remembers, even faintly, the small girls who hung on her every word that July.

Trading day at the canteen was when we lined up with grimy quarters from the bottom of our duffel bags and bought packets of fizzy candy and stamps for our letters home. The line snaked across the dusty yard, and the sun beat down, and we were absolutely, wholly happy, though we did not know to call it that yet.

I once got homesick so badly during the second week that I asked the nurse if I could call my mother, and she let me sit in her tiny office with the rotary phone while I cried. My mother told me to stay, that I would thank her later, and she was right, of course, as she so often was about so many things.

The last morning we packed our trunks in a kind of stunned silence, and our parents arrived in dusty station wagons, and we sat on the lawn waiting and refusing to look at each other in case it made us cry. I miss the way endings felt that absolute when I was young.

Halloween on our block was a community production. The Petersons gave out full-sized candy bars, the Wallaces always had the front porch decorated with real pumpkins they had grown, and old Mrs. Garner sat on her stoop with a bowl of pennies and homemade popcorn balls wrapped in waxed paper. We knew which houses were the good ones and we mapped our routes the way generals planned campaigns.

My mother made my costumes from things she found in the rag bag, and even the year I was a robot built out of two cardboard boxes painted silver and a foil-covered colander, I never felt anything less than spectacular walking up to our neighbors' doors.

There was a particular shade of October dusk, that smoky violet that settled over the leaves just before the streetlights came on, and we ran through it in pillowcases that grew heavier by the block. I have not seen that exact color of sky in years.

We always ended the night dumping our hauls onto the living room rug under the lamp and trading like little merchants, my brother holding Tootsie Rolls hostage for the Reese's that he knew I prized above all things. He always won. He still would, I think, if we ever sat down to it again.

The Andersons' yard had a fog machine and a recording of howling that they played from a tape deck on the porch, and we were small enough to find it genuinely terrifying. I miss being scared by a tape deck. I miss being small enough for that to be enough.

Our pumpkins sat on the front step for weeks before the thirty-first, and on the morning of, my father would line us up at the kitchen table with newspaper and spoons and we would carve them together, the kitchen smelling of cool flesh and seeds that my mother roasted with salt.

Older kids in the neighborhood threw eggs and toilet paper sometimes, and I remember being thrilled to be considered too small to be a target. I felt enclosed in a kind of golden bubble of childhood, untouchable, certain of every door I would knock on.

My father always came with us up until the year I turned ten, when I declared myself old enough to go with my friends. He stood at the end of the driveway and waved as we ran off, and I remember the way he looked smaller from down the block, smaller and almost a little sad, though I did not understand it then.

There was always one house with the porch light off, and we would dare each other to ring the bell anyway, hearts hammering. That house belonged to a widow whose husband had died that summer, and I understand it now, but I did not then, and I think of her sometimes with great tenderness.

The candy lasted until Thanksgiving in a brown paper bag on top of the refrigerator, slowly thinning, the chocolate going slightly chalky. I would climb up on the counter when no one was looking and choose carefully, like a curator in a small museum of my own remembered triumphs.

Sunday dinner at my grandparents' was an institution. We arrived at one o'clock sharp, and my grandmother always met us at the door in an apron flecked with flour, smelling of yeast and something herby, and the house warm in a way that no house I have lived in since has ever been warm.

The table was always set with the good china that came out only on Sundays and holidays, and my grandfather carved the roast with a long bone-handled knife that had belonged to his father. He sharpened it on a stone every Saturday night, a small ritual that I did not appreciate until much later.

There were always too many of us. Aunts and uncles and second cousins and someone's friend from church squeezed shoulder to shoulder, the kids at the card table in the next room because there was never enough space. I would trade my whole calendar now for one more chair at that table.

After the meal my grandfather would retire to his armchair with the newspaper and his glasses pushed down on his nose, and within ten minutes he would be asleep. The grandfather clock ticked, the women laughed in the kitchen, and the boys went out to throw a ball in the yard, and the world was as it should be.

My grandmother's gravy was a thing of legend, and she would never write down the recipe, claiming it had to be done by feel. When she died, the recipe died with her, and now my mother and I attempt versions every Thanksgiving that come close but never quite arrive, which I think is exactly how my grandmother would have wanted it.

The dessert was always something with rhubarb or apples from the trees in the back, served in glass dishes with a small pour of cream, and the children were allowed coffee for the first time at that table, watered down with milk in a teacup that had a chip on its handle.

I remember the patterned wallpaper in the dining room, faintly yellowed from years of cigarette smoke before they quit, and a print of a hunting scene that hung crooked because the wire had stretched. Nothing in that house ever quite matched, and everything in it belonged exactly where it was.

The driveway was crowded with cars by half past noon, and we kids would press our faces to the front window watching for our cousins to arrive. The minute they pulled in we sprinted out, our church shoes still on, and the dirt got into the patent leather and our mothers would scold us later, half-heartedly.

After dinner the women cleared and the men sat and the children were free to disappear, and I would slip away to my grandmother's sewing room and open the drawer where she kept buttons in a tin coffee can, and I would pour them out on the rug and sort them by color for an hour at a time, perfectly content.

When we left, my grandmother always sent us home with leftovers wrapped in foil and pressed into our hands at the door, as if she knew the week ahead would be long and the world outside her house cold. Sometimes I open my refrigerator now and miss those foil packets so much my throat aches.

The milk truck came down our street before dawn three times a week, and I remember the soft chink of glass bottles being set down on the front step and the diesel rumble of the engine moving on. My mother would open the door in her dressing gown and the cold air would rush in and the milk would be inside almost before I had woken up.

Our milkman's name was Harold and he wore a white cap and a uniform with his name stitched on the chest, and on my birthday he always left an extra carton of chocolate milk in the box without my mother asking. I have not had chocolate milk taste like that since.

The cream rose to the top of the bottles in those days, in a thick yellow plug under the foil cap, and my father would skim it off with a spoon for his coffee on Sunday mornings while my mother shook her head at the sight, and the kitchen would smell of toast and percolator coffee and that particular cream.

We left our empties out the night before in a metal box on the porch, and washing them was my job on Sunday afternoons. I would rinse and rinse with cold water and line them up like little soldiers, and I remember the satisfaction of seeing them clear and gleaming, ready for Harold's return.

In winter the cream sometimes froze and pushed the foil cap up two inches above the rim of the bottle, like a little frozen turban, and we children would race down in our pajamas to see it before our mother could bring the bottles in. The sight delighted us in a way I cannot quite communicate.

When the dairy went out of business in the late seventies, my mother kept one of the bottles on a shelf in the pantry. It was still there when we sold the house twenty years later, and I took it home and washed it and now it sits on my own shelf, a small monument to a morning sound I cannot get back.

Harold knew everyone on the route. He knew my grandmother had broken her hip and he started bringing her milk to the door, and he knew the Hendersons were going through a hard time and he forgave the bill twice. The man had a route and he had a community, and these were not different things to him.

On Saturday mornings I sometimes flagged down the truck and Harold let me ride in the passenger seat to the end of the block, and I felt like I had been admitted to a secret society of grown-ups. The cab smelled of pipe tobacco and faintly of milk, and the floor was littered with the little paper receipts he wrote out by hand.

Harold's truck broke down once in front of our house and my father went out in his slippers to help him push it to the curb, and they stood talking for an hour, and I watched them from the upstairs window. Two men in white shirts in the early light, talking about nothing in particular. It was the most ordinary thing in the world. I have been chasing the ordinariness of it ever since.

The bottles had the dairy's name embossed on the side in raised glass, and when you held one up to the kitchen light you could see the letters glow faintly. We had no idea we were the last generation to see those bottles. We thought they would always be there.

The municipal pool was the center of our summer universe. We arrived at ten in the morning when it opened and we did not leave until they made us leave at five, and we were the color of a tea-stained handkerchief by August, the chlorine having turned our hair some shade of green that my mother despaired of.

The snack bar sold frozen Charleston Chews and grape Popsicles that turned your tongue purple for hours, and we negotiated their purchase out of the change at the bottom of our beach bags, counting nickels in a small puddle on the concrete.

Adult swim came every hour on the hour, and we sat on the hot edge of the pool with our feet in the water, watching the grown-ups do slow laps and wishing the fifteen minutes would end. I remember the precise feeling of the white-hot cement on the backs of my thighs and the smell of coconut sunscreen on my mother's arm next to me.

Becky Daniels could dive off the high board the summer we were nine, and the rest of us spent that year trying to work up the courage. I remember the climb up that hot metal ladder, the sky tilting, the water looking impossibly far away, and the absolute silence that fell over the pool when someone finally jumped.

There was a lifeguard named Steve who looked like a movie star to every twelve-year-old girl in the county, and we all took turns pretending to drown in the shallow end so he might lean down from his chair. He never did. He was reading a book about Vietnam. I think of him now and hope he made it through, hope he is well.

Friday nights they did dive-in movies, projecting onto a sheet hung from the chain-link fence, and we floated on our backs watching The Sandlot for the fourth time that summer while the moths circled the projector and the bats came out over the parking lot.

The walk home in the late afternoon was a particular kind of holy. Hair wet, towels heavy, the sun lower and gentler than it had been at noon, the cicadas going, and the smell of supper starting from kitchen windows along the way. I would go back to that walk if I could go anywhere.

We had a code of pool conduct that no adult ever taught us but every kid knew. Where to leave your towel, when to do a cannonball and when not to, who got the inner tube next. The rules were elaborate, fiercely enforced, and entirely fair, and I have never since been part of a society that worked so well.

The pool closed Labor Day weekend, and we lined up on the deck and watched the lifeguards take the lane ropes out and we all knew, with a kind of grief we did not have the words for, that another summer had ended. I have that feeling every September still, decades later, without quite knowing why.

They tore the old pool down in 2003 and put up a splash park with shorter hours and no high dive, and I drove past it last year and could not bring myself to stop. Somewhere underneath all that new rubberized matting is the cement I used to lie on, sun-warm, while my friends shouted and the radio played the same five songs all summer long.

My first car was a 1978 Buick LeSabre the color of weak tea, inherited from a great-aunt who had stopped driving. It had a bench seat in the front and an AM radio that picked up two stations on a good day, and I loved that car the way you love a friend who knows all your secrets.

The vinyl seats stuck to the back of my legs in summer and the heater took twenty minutes to warm up in winter, and the trunk could hold an entire household if you packed carefully, which I did, the night I moved out of my parents' house at nineteen.

We drove that car to the Grand Canyon the summer after high school, four of us with a cooler in the back seat and a road atlas held together with tape. The air conditioning went out somewhere in New Mexico and we drove the rest of the way with the windows down, sunburned and laughing, and I have never been happier in any vehicle since.

I sold the Buick to pay for textbooks my sophomore year, and I cried in the parking lot of the dealership after the new owner drove off in it. He waved out the window as he turned onto the road, and I waved back, and I have thought about that car at least once a week ever since.

There was a particular smell to that car, a mixture of old vinyl and pine air freshener and the faint mint of my great-aunt's chewing gum, which I found in the glove compartment when I cleaned it out and could not bring myself to throw away. I still have the pack, somewhere, in a drawer of small saved things.

My father taught me to drive in that car in the empty parking lot of the old Sears that had closed the year before, and he was patient in a way I had not known him to be patient, and I learned to back into a parking space between two trash dumpsters that he set up as markers. He was very proud of me.

On long drives I used to talk to the car, and I cannot quite explain why, except that it seemed to be listening. I named it Henrietta and I would tell Henrietta about the boy I liked or the test I was worried about, and I would arrive at my destination feeling lighter for having spoken.

The first kiss I ever got happened in the front seat of that Buick, in the parking lot of a Dairy Queen, with the engine off and the radio still playing on the battery. I was seventeen and I thought I would die of it. I almost did. The world has been a quieter place ever since.

My mother packed me sandwiches for the long drive to college, and they sat on the bench seat next to me, wrapped in waxed paper, alongside a thermos of coffee and a tape my brother had made for me of his favorite songs. I ate them slowly, eight hours on the road, weeping at intervals.

I parked Henrietta in front of my dormitory my freshman year and a girl named Mira walked by and said, this is the prettiest car I have ever seen, and we have been friends for almost thirty years now. None of it would have happened without that car. I am grateful for it still.

We caught fireflies in mason jars with holes punched in the lids, and we kept them on the nightstand and watched them blink until we fell asleep. In the morning we let them go before they could die, opening the lid in the wet grass while the dew soaked our pajamas.

There were more fireflies then. I am not imagining it. The whole back field would light up after supper, hundreds of small drifting lanterns, and we would run through them with our arms out, and the dogs would chase us, and our mothers called us in long after dark and forgave us, mostly, when we came.

My grandfather called them lightning bugs and told us, with the same wistful look he used for almost everything, that they were the souls of the people he had known. I did not understand him then. I do now, very precisely, and I miss him terribly.

My cousin Renee could catch a firefly in her cupped hands without crushing it, a skill I never managed, and she would open her hands so I could see the small green pulse of it on her palm before she let it go. She passed away last spring. I think of her hands often.

The dew on the lawn at firefly time was always cold against bare feet, and we wore sweatshirts over our shorts because the air had turned, and the grown-ups sat on the porch with iced tea and we could hear their voices but not their words, and that was exactly how it should have been.

I took my own daughter out to catch fireflies last summer at my parents' house, and we found three, all evening, and she was thrilled with them. I did not tell her about the meadows full of them when I was her age. Some things are not for telling.

There was a particular quality to the dusk in late June, that long stretched-out hour when the sky kept refusing to go fully dark and the fireflies started up one by one, and I remember the absolute belief that the summer would never end, that I would never go back to school, that the world had set itself to this and would stay.

We held contests to see who could catch the most, and we counted them carefully into our jars, and at the end of the night my grandmother always declared a tie so no one would go to bed disappointed. I thought she was being indecisive at the time. I see now that she was being kind.

My father once told me you could smear the glowing part on your finger and it would shine for a few seconds, and I tried it, and the firefly died, and I cried, and my father felt terrible. We did not speak of it again, and I never killed another one, and I think of that small dead thing every time I see a firefly now.

The last firefly of the season was always sometime in mid-August, and you never knew which one it would be at the time, and only later you realized you had not seen one in a week. That kind of ending happens with so many things. You don't know it has happened until it has been gone for a while.

The front porch of my grandparents' house ran the full width of the building and was screened against the bugs, and there was a creaking swing on chains at one end and a row of wicker chairs at the other, and that porch was where the real conversations happened, after dinner, into the night.

I remember the soft thud of June bugs against the screen and the squeak of the swing chains and my grandfather's pipe and the distant sound of a freight train somewhere across the river, and I would lie on the floorboards looking up at the porch ceiling, which was painted a pale blue to keep wasps from nesting.

Neighbors walked by in the evening and they would stop and lean on the porch railing and talk for half an hour. They had nowhere they had to be. There was no television in the kitchen calling them home. The conversation was the point, and so was the slow drift of the evening, and so was the cold sweating glass of iced tea.

My grandmother kept a pitcher of lemonade with mint from her garden in the porch cooler, and she refilled it every couple of hours, and the glass jar of it sweat onto the painted tray on the side table, and I remember the round wet ring it left behind, exactly.

I have lived in apartments my entire adult life, and the absence of a porch is one of the small daily griefs I have not learned to make peace with. I would give a great deal for a screened porch and a swing and a quiet evening with the people I loved being around again.

We slept on the porch in the worst heat of August, on cots my grandfather pulled out of the shed, and we listened to the cicadas and the screen door slapping shut in the breeze and the soft electric snap of the bug zapper at the corner of the yard. I have not slept that well since.

My aunts would gather there on Saturday afternoons with shelling peas in a paper bag and a colander between them, and they would talk for hours about people I had never met and laugh until they cried, and I sat on the swing and listened and felt initiated into something profound.

After my grandfather died, my grandmother stopped sitting on the porch in the evenings, and we knew without saying so that the world had changed in a permanent way. The swing stayed. The chairs stayed. But the porch was no longer the same porch, and the evenings were no longer the same evenings.

I drove past the house a few years ago and a young family had bought it, and the porch furniture was bright plastic and the screen had been replaced with new bright mesh and there was a baby playing on the floor where I used to lie and watch the ceiling. I was glad for them and very sad for me.

The porch had a number stenciled on a board nailed to one post, painted black on white, and the paint had cracked into a particular pattern that I traced with my finger on summer afternoons. I would know that crack anywhere. It was as familiar to me as my own handwriting.

Our living room television was a wooden console TV that weighed approximately as much as a small car, and the picture took a moment to come up after you turned the knob, and the antenna on top had two extendable rods that we adjusted with a kind of solemn precision to get a clean channel.

We had aluminum foil wrapped around the tips of the rabbit ears for better reception, and on stormy nights one of us had to stand and hold the antenna in just the right position for the rest of the family to see the screen. I was the youngest, so the job was usually mine. I did not mind.

The set had a soft hum when it warmed up, and a smell of warm dust and old electronics, and after you turned it off the white dot in the center of the screen lingered for a minute or two before fading. I miss that dot. It felt like the picture was saying goodnight.

There were three channels and a UHF dial that mostly gave you static, and on Sunday nights the whole family watched the same show at the same time because there was nothing else, and I think we were better off for it, though I would not say so out loud to a person under thirty.

When the test pattern came on at midnight, the television played the national anthem and then went to a high whine and the colored bars, and you knew that was it, the day was over, the country had gone to sleep. I cannot fully convey what that felt like, the certainty of it, but I miss it.

My father had a small black-and-white TV in his workshop, and on the weekends I would sit on a stool next to him and we would watch the ballgame together with the sound very low because my mother said the static gave her a headache, and he would explain the rules to me as the innings went by.

We watched the moon landing on that television in the summer of sixty-nine, and my mother let us stay up far past our bedtime, and she made cocoa, and we did not understand what we were seeing but we knew we were supposed to remember it. And I do. I remember the cocoa, and the static, and the small grainy figure on the screen.

The repair man came once a year to replace the tubes, and he brought a wooden case full of vacuum tubes packed in straw, and he laid them out on the rug like a doctor laying out instruments, and I watched in absolute fascination as he diagnosed our television and fixed it. His name was Mr. Polk. He smelled of cigars.

I got up early on Saturdays to watch cartoons, and the picture would flicker when our refrigerator kicked on, and I would jiggle the antenna and hold my breath, and the picture would come back, and Scooby-Doo would resume his business and the morning would unfold as ordained.

We gave the old console TV away to a young couple down the street when we got our first color set, and they hauled it off in the back of a pickup truck, and I watched it go from the front window. I felt as though we had handed off a member of the family. In a way, I think we had.

Our school playground was built over a hill, and the slide went down so steep that I once flew off the bottom and skidded across the gravel and my knee bled and I cried, and a fourth-grader named Marcus carried me to the nurse, and I loved him forever after for that one act of unsolicited kindness.

The monkey bars had a particular smell of warm metal in the sun, and our palms came away orange with rust by the end of recess, and we wiped them on the backs of our jeans and went back inside still smelling of that hot iron.

The swings were the prize possession of the playground, and there was an unwritten code about how to claim one, and how long you could stay, and whether you had to give it up if someone older asked. The system was completely fair and never discussed and I will never see anything like it again.

We played a game called four-square with a red rubber ball and a chalked grid on the asphalt, and I cannot remember the rules now but I remember the absolute seriousness with which they were enforced and the political shifts of who was king of the square in any given week.

There was a wooden train near the kindergarten end, and the paint was always peeling, and a generation of small hands had worn the seats smooth. My mother had played on that same train when she was little, and so had her mother, and when they tore it down to put up a plastic structure in the nineties, I felt the loss of it as if it had been a relative.

We had a teacher on duty during recess who carried a metal whistle on a string around her neck, and the blast of it ended recess every day at exactly ten-thirty, and I can still hear the sound, sharp and final, cutting across the laughter and the shouting like a kind of small mourning.

Tetherball was the cool game in fourth grade, and there was always a line, and the seventh-grader who ran it accepted bribes of fruit roll-ups to let you skip ahead. I gave up so many fruit roll-ups to that boy. I am not sure I have ever made a worse investment, or a happier one.

In winter we sledded down the hill on plastic trays from the cafeteria, even though we were not supposed to, and we hid them in the bushes at the end of recess and retrieved them the next day. The cafeteria staff knew. They never said a word. I think of them with the deepest affection.

Sarah Hill broke her arm falling off the climbing structure in third grade, and we all signed her cast at the end of the day, and I drew a heart and she drew a heart on my forearm with the same blue pen. We had not spoken in years when she got married, but I went to the wedding anyway.

The bell rang at the end of recess and we lined up in two rows by class, and we walked back into the building dragging our feet, and the air-conditioned cool of the hallway hit us like a wall after the heat of the asphalt, and we sat back down at our desks already counting the minutes until tomorrow.

We painted our faces in school colors and yelled until our voices were gone and went out for pancakes afterward, win or lose, at the diner on Main Street that stayed open late on Fridays just for us. The waitresses knew our drink orders by senior year.

Tommy Reilly threw the touchdown pass in the championship game my senior year, and the whole stadium rose up in one motion, and I have not felt anything quite like the noise it made, the absolute unity of two thousand people losing their minds together. I think of it often.

The boys had their letter jackets and the girls borrowed them and wore them over their dresses on Fridays before the game, and there was a precise social mathematics to which boy you were dating based on whose jacket was hanging in your locker, and we took it very seriously, and we were right to.

Halftime was for the band, and our band was small and earnest and they did formations on the field that were always more ambitious than their numbers could support, and we cheered for them louder than we cheered for the team because they were our friends and we knew exactly how hard they had practiced.

My uncle had a Polaroid camera that came out at every birthday party, and the picture would slide out the front of it with a mechanical whir, and we would all stand around staring at the white square as the colors came up, and someone always shook it though I have since learned this was not necessary.

There is a Polaroid of me at four, holding a stuffed elephant and wearing a yellow dress with a stain on the front, and my mother kept it in her wallet for forty years, and the colors went strange and the edges faded, and her face when she showed it to people did not fade at all.

We were not the family that posed for pictures. We were caught mid-laugh, mid-sentence, with mouths full of cake and eyes half-closed, and that is what makes the Polaroids precious now, that they did not let anyone look ready for them.

I have a box of Polaroids from my grandmother's house, given to me when she moved into the assisted living, and most of them are of people I cannot identify. They are her cousins, her bridge partners, her old neighbors. I keep them anyway. Someone should remember the small Friday gatherings in the den of 1973.

The film for those cameras was expensive, and my uncle treated each shot like a small act of significance, and the result was that the photos that exist are concentrated, careful, framed. There are no thousand digital images of any single afternoon. There are three Polaroids, and they are gold.

My grandmother labeled the back of every Polaroid in pencil, in her tidy script that I would know anywhere. Birthday, June 1974. Easter at Maud's house, 1971. She knew what she was doing. She was building us an archive. We did not appreciate it until she was gone.

The travel section was my favorite when I was older, and I would clip articles about Paris or Rome and tape them to my bedroom wall, and I believed firmly that I would visit every place I clipped. I have gotten to most of them. I am still working on the rest.

Mrs. Bell was my teacher, and she had white hair already at thirty-eight, and she wore a smock with deep pockets full of small things she could pull out at the right moment, and she got down on the floor with us, and she remembered everyone's name by the end of the first morning.

We sat in a circle on a rag rug and sang a song I had never heard before, about a duck named Donald, and I learned it in two repetitions and I went home and sang it for my father, and he learned it too, and he sang it back to me at bedtime for years afterward.

There was milk at snack time in tiny waxed cartons that you had to learn to open by pushing the sides in, and a graham cracker that broke neatly along the perforation, and the whole ceremony of it felt very serious, the small ritual of the snack.

When the bell rang at the end of the day I was almost reluctant to leave, and I told my mother so, and she looked at me with such pride and such grief at once, and I see that expression on my own face now sometimes, watching my children walk into their own days.

sentence: The bandstand still stands. The concerts still happen, every other Wednesday now instead of every week, and the band is smaller and older and the audience is smaller and older, and I went last summer and sat on the grass alone and listened to a march I knew by heart, and I wept a little, quietly, into my sleeve.

subtopic: the old bandstand in the park
sentence: I climbed up onto the bandstand once when I was little, after a concert, and stood where the conductor stood, and looked out at the empty lawn littered with abandoned napkins, and I felt enormous and very small at once. The wood was warm under my bare feet. My grandfather watched from the grass and did not call me down.

subtopic: the old bandstand in the park
sentence: There is a plaque on the bandstand now with my grandfather's name on it, in among a list of clarinetists who served the band for over a decade, and I touch it whenever I pass through that park, and I am not sure whether I am greeting him or being greeted by him, but the touching of it is the point.
